item.title: Ofala Festival: The Unbroken Spirit Of Onitsha And A Monarch’s Silver Jubilee
item.description: For a week, the royal palace descends into a sacred silence. Behind closed doors, the “King of Onitsha” becomes invisible as he continues to commune with the ancestors and negotiate his people’s fortunes. However, the first rhythmic thud of the Egwu Ota – the ancient royal war drums – reverberates through the Eze Chima Square, shattering that silence and ending the seclusion called “Inye Ukwu n’Nlo Eze.” ﻿ Then, Ndichie (the council of red-cap chiefs), dressed in crimson caps and white robes, surges forward, parting only when a bronze sword catches the afternoon sun. That signals the arrival of the Obi of Onitsha, His Majesty Igwe Nnaemeka Alfred Achebe. This grand entry marks the climax of the Ofala Festival, a 500-year-old cultural event celebrated by the Onitsha people of Anambra State. It is a rite of renewal for the Obi and a renewal of bonds between the throne and king and the people of Onitsha. Here, the Obi presents himself to the people after a time of seclusion and spiritual cleansing to show he is alive, healthy, and still has the mandate to lead his people. Obi of Onitsha, Nnaemeka Alfred Achebe, acknowledges cheers from the crowd at the 2026 Ofala Festival in Onitsha, Anambra State. As the Obi of Onitsha steps into the square, he performs three rhythmic dances before his people – a move that indicates prosperity, stability, and continuity of the land for another native calendar year. But the 2026 edition, celebrated in October like other years, marked a historic milestone for Onitsha people: it was the 25th Ofala Festival in the reign of Igwe Achebe. The year’s celebration came with the theme, “Igba Mbo, Iga N’Iru” (Strive and Advance) and was a colourful event that recreated the rich heritage of the Onitsha people. As dignitaries, hundreds of visitors gathered at the Ezechima Square; the Onitsha high chiefs swayed in their full ceremonial regalia, showcasing the traditional Egwu Ota dance and their loyalty to the Obi of Onitsha. “In the olden days, these high chiefs were the warriors we had in our villages,” the Anambra State Commissioner for Transport, Edward Ibuzoh, said after watching them charm the crowd with their dance steps. “These are the people that represent the village, and that is why every Ofala, they come with their people… to pay homage to the Agbogidi—to tell him that they are strong and vibrant, willing, and ready to serve.” For the Senator representing Anambra North, Tony Nwoye, the event, which coincides with Igwe Achebe’s 25 years on the throne, is a testament to the king’s leadership. “The Igwe has done his best to bring Igbo across the world to be together,” Nwoye said, “and he has done his best to bring about the development of infrastructure in Onitsha. That is why we respect him.” The Ofala Festival has a cross-continental pull. For the 2026 edition, American scholar and author, Professor Richard Henderson, was seated among the dignitaries. Henderson, the author of The King in Every Man, travelled about 12,1
item.dc:creator: Emmanuel Egobiambu
item.content:encoded: For a week, the royal palace descends into a sacred silence. Behind closed doors, the “King of Onitsha” becomes invisible as he continues to commune with the ancestors and negotiate his people’s fortunes. However, the first rhythmic thud of the Egwu Ota – the ancient royal war drums – reverberates through the Eze Chima Square, shattering that silence and ending the seclusion called “Inye Ukwu n’Nlo Eze.” ﻿ Then, Ndichie (the council of red-cap chiefs), dressed in crimson caps and white robes, surges forward, parting only when a bronze sword catches the afternoon sun. That signals the arrival of the Obi of Onitsha, His Majesty Igwe Nnaemeka Alfred Achebe. This grand entry marks the climax of the Ofala Festival, a 500-year-old cultural event celebrated by the Onitsha people of Anambra State. It is a rite of renewal for the Obi and a renewal of bonds between the throne and king and the people of Onitsha. Here, the Obi presents himself to the people after a time of seclusion and spiritual cleansing to show he is alive, healthy, and still has the mandate to lead his people. Obi of Onitsha, Nnaemeka Alfred Achebe, acknowledges cheers from the crowd at the 2026 Ofala Festival in Onitsha, Anambra State. As the Obi of Onitsha steps into the square, he performs three rhythmic dances before his people – a move that indicates prosperity, stability, and continuity of the land for another native calendar year. But the 2026 edition, celebrated in October like other years, marked a historic milestone for Onitsha people: it was the 25th Ofala Festival in the reign of Igwe Achebe. The year’s celebration came with the theme, “Igba Mbo, Iga N’Iru” (Strive and Advance) and was a colourful event that recreated the rich heritage of the Onitsha people. As dignitaries, hundreds of visitors gathered at the Ezechima Square; the Onitsha high chiefs swayed in their full ceremonial regalia, showcasing the traditional Egwu Ota dance and their loyalty to the Obi of Onitsha. “In the olden days, these high chiefs were the warriors we had in our villages,” the Anambra State Commissioner for Transport, Edward Ibuzoh, said after watching them charm the crowd with their dance steps. “These are the people that represent the village, and that is why every Ofala, they come with their people… to pay homage to the Agbogidi—to tell him that they are strong and vibrant, willing, and ready to serve.” For the Senator representing Anambra North, Tony Nwoye, the event, which coincides with Igwe Achebe’s 25 years on the throne, is a testament to the king’s leadership. “The Igwe has done his best to bring Igbo across the world to be together,” Nwoye said, “and he has done his best to bring about the development of infrastructure in Onitsha. That is why we respect him.” The Ofala Festival has a cross-continental pull. For the 2026 edition, American scholar and author, Professor Richard Henderson, was seated among the dignitaries. Henderson, the author of The King in Every Man, travelled about 12,194 kilometres from Tucson, Arizona, to experience the festivities 60 years after his first research visit in the 1960s. “I am astonished at how elaborate it has become—richer and more vital than it was,” Henderson said. “It was the most amazing culture I had encountered, which is why I spent so much time writing it up. But now, it has become even more exciting and glorious.” Obi of Onitsha, Nnaemeka Alfred Achebe, acknowledges cheers from the crowd at the 2025 Ofala Festival in Onitsha, Anambra State. Like other editions, the 2026 Ofala Festival offered more than a celebratory value. As the moral compass of the Onitsha community and one of the most respected monarchs in the country, when the Obi stood on the podium, his message transcended the immediate community. Addressing the nation, he asked President Bola Tinubu to resolve the worsening economic hardships in Nigeria. “Let me briefly mention the hardship and insecurity that have worsened steadily in the country,” the Obi said. “We join in prayer that the government will take urgent measures to alleviate the pain of ordinary citizens caused by the macroeconomic measures being pursued.” With the 2027 elections months away, he also asked residents of the South-East region, which includes Enugu, Anambra, Imo, Abia and Ebonyi states, to shun voter apathy. “Still on the national elections, I call on the people of the South-East States to shake off their historical apathy towards elections,” the 85-year-old told the gathering. “We cannot stay away from elections and turn around to complain of marginalisation. In democracy, all votes count. Therefore, we must come out and vote for our candidates”. With over 500 years of history, the Ofala remains a vital celebration of Onitsha’s royal heritage, preserving cultural identity and uniting residents, visitors, and admirers worldwide. item.title: Politics in 'materialist terms': Gen Z in Albania, Italy, France and India protesting for 'fairness'
item.description: Jean-Emile Jammine is pleased to welcome Gökçe Tuncel, Sociologist and post-doctoral researcher associated with the Université Paris-Est Créteil (UPEC). For Tuncel, the wave of youth-led protests across France, Albania, India and Italy reveals more than a succession of localized grievances. It signals the emergence of a political consciousness shaped by material insecurity, institutional disillusionment and an increasingly explicit demand for solidarity and social justice. "What is really striking about this Gen Z movement is how clearly young people see their material conditions," Tuncel observes.

item.title: Is el clásico still the world’s biggest match? Three questions before Barcelona v Real Madrid
item.description: The fixture’s relevance waned as the Messi-Ronaldo rivalry faded. Can Lamine Yamal and Mbappé lift it into a new era? For the best part of a decade, el clásico was more than just soccer’s biggest fixture. It was the defining narrative. At the peak of the Lionel Messi v Cristiano Ronaldo era, there were clásicos everywhere. Yes, when the two historic rivals clashed on the pitch, but also in the voting for the Ballon d’Or every year and in so much of the discourse around the sport. As the Messi-Ronaldo rivalry faded, though, so too did the clásico ’s relevance. This isn’t to say matches between Barcelona and Real Madrid no longer matter. They always have and always will. In 2026, however, it’s difficult to measure a clásico ’s standing. Is it still the sport’s biggest fixture? Continue reading...
item.dc:creator: Graham Ruthven
item.content:encoded: The fixture’s relevance waned as the Messi-Ronaldo rivalry faded. Can Lamine Yamal and Mbappé lift it into a new era? For the best part of a decade, el clásico was more than just soccer’s biggest fixture. It was the defining narrative. At the peak of the Lionel Messi v Cristiano Ronaldo era, there were clásicos everywhere. Yes, when the two historic rivals clashed on the pitch, but also in the voting for the Ballon d’Or every year and in so much of the discourse around the sport. As the Messi-Ronaldo rivalry faded, though, so too did the clásico ’s relevance. This isn’t to say matches between Barcelona and Real Madrid no longer matter. They always have and always will. In 2026, however, it’s difficult to measure a clásico ’s standing. Is it still the sport’s biggest fixture? Continue reading...

item.title: Veteran Nollywood Actor Francis Duru Passes Away at 57 | Read Family Statement
item.description: Veteran Nollywood actor Francis Duru has passed away at the age of 57. Photo Credit: Francis Duru/Instagram The Nigerian film industry has been thrown into mourning following the sad passing of veteran Nollywood actor, director,and academic, Francis Duru . The respected movie star passed away at the age of 57 following a brief illness, leaving behind a incredible legacy that spans over three decades of memorable performances across television and cinema. Sharing the heartbreaking news with fans and well-wishers on his official Instagram page, his family released a moving statement: We, the family of Francis Duru, regret to announce his passing following a brief illness. We appreciate your prayers, love, and understanding. May his soul rest in perfect peace. Amen. A true pioneer of modern Nollywood, Francis Duru made his screen debut back in 1989 in the feature Missing Mark , before shooting to nationwide fame for his unforgettable portrayal of Ahanna in Amaka Igwe ’s 1995 classic Rattlesnake . Over the years, he cemented his status as a household name with stellar roles in acclaimed movies such as Blood Money , Mama Sunday , Total Control , Home in Exile , Mboputa , and Stigma . Beyond his stellar career in front of the camera, Duru was a dedicated academic holding a degree in Theatre Arts from the University of Port Harcourt, and a passionate advocate who served as a United Nations Ambassador of Peace and as interim President of the Actors Guild of Nigeria (AGN). Francis Duru is survived by his loving wife, Adokiye Duru , whom he married in 2003, and their children The post Veteran Nollywood Actor Francis Duru Passes Away at 57 | Read Family Statement appeared first on BellaNaija - Showcasing Africa to the world. Read today! .

item.title: Naomi Ackie Was Anything but Basic in Sculptural Schiaparelli at Paris Fashion Week
item.description: Naomi Ackie Naomi Ackie has been delivering some serious fashion moments lately, and her appearance at the Schiaparelli show during Paris Fashion Week is another one for the books. The British-Grenadian actress wore a striking black, single-sleeved gown that perfectly captured the house’s surrealist sensibility. Thousands of finely worked pleats created an almost liquid effect, hugging her figure before falling into a dramatic thigh-high slit. But what really makes this look special is the exaggerated sleeve, which gives the otherwise sleek silhouette an architectural quality. Naomi has worn the brand a few times, and we love how she always embraces the brand’s aesthetic without letting it overwhelm her. The sculptural statement earrings and signature face-motif clutch brought just the right amount of the house’s eccentricity, while her slicked-back ponytail kept the overall look sharp and modern. item.title: Beware the claw: Do you want to win the bunny or reboot Android?
item.description: Today's victim of the bork fairy is a claw machine that even Android seems to have rejected for its alleged unfairness. And Google, as we all know, is all about fairness. Eagle-eyed Register reader Scott spotted the stricken machine in an arcade adjacent to a roller rink, a place our reader visited with a friend and described as "something my currently bruised body reminds me I hadn't done for about 20 years." We assume they were talking about roller-skating, and not the exertions of accompanying their pal. The machine itself is a recent iteration of the infamous claw machine, which has spent a century emptying players' pockets in exchange for frustration and the very occasional reward of tat. Infamously, the devices are sometimes rigged so the claw's strength varies between turns, and in several parts of the world, gambling laws cover the machines. However, the only gambling to be done here is on whether or not Android will boot. Like so many players in the past, the machine has lost this bet, and an Android Recovery Console is on show. We're not sure who lennie022 is – perhaps a user or perhaps some corporate account – but the words "release-keys" probably don't belong on top of the device. They're unlikely to entice any everyday players to part with cash. The usual recovery menu is hidden thanks to the dimensions of the screen. If something like this comes up on a mobile device, the volume up and down buttons tend to be used for navigation. In this case, the joystick is presumably the only I/O method, and the selected option would be pot-luck. Which, we guess, is the whole point. More discreet is the screen below the machine which, rather than encourage a player to grip the sweaty handle, is now plaintively asking for some removable storage (we've seen enough electronic gizmos to know what those pictograms mean) on a blue background that would bring a tear to the eye of many a Microsoft engineer. In fact, something that looks a bit like a blue screen of death and a borked Android? Perhaps this combination would lure an engineer to the controls… Sure, there's no obvious place to stick removable storage or attach a keyboard. But a waggle of the joystick couldn't hurt, could it? Perhaps one more? Dammit. Now we're restarting Android, when all we wanted was that pink bunny. ®

item.title: Vendor-affiliated AI agent tech gets adopted by friendly, funded foundation
item.description: The Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF) has been entrusted with stewardship of four additional AI projects in the hope of broadening the set of vendor-neutral tools for making AI agents. The AAIF was founded in December 2025 under the auspices of the Linux Foundation as a vendor-neutral organization for the benefit of AI companies more interested in riding a tide that lifts all boats than making waves. It launched with three projects under its supervision: Model Context Protocol (MCP), goose, and AGENTS.md. With the four new adoptees, there are now 10 projects sheltering under the AAIF's wings. The donor organizations – Alibaba, Anthropic, Hugging Face, and OpenAI – have handed over control of OpenSandbox, Agent Skills, OpenEnv, and Open Responses respectively. Each of these projects provides functions that developers of AI agents – which typically combine models, tools, and a task loop – may find helpful. And having a more or less agreed-upon blueprint for implementation tends to make deployment easier and more predictable, at least until your AI agent unexpectedly ransacks some third-party organization. OpenSandbox provides a way to constrain or sandbox the capabilities of AI agents using various client SDKs, tools, protocols, lifecycle hooks, container runtimes, and assorted in-sandbox execution components. Agent Skills outlines a format for text descriptions that guide AI agents through specified tasks more effectively. It provides context that helps agents accomplish their goals. "We’re committed to keeping Agent Skills open, community-driven, and vendor-neutral," said Anthropic, an AAIF co-founder, in a blog post . OpenEnv offers a containerized service for creating reinforcement learning environments that can be built without much trouble, can interoperate, and can scale to meet demanding testing. And Open Responses is an open API specification for building LLM interfaces that can work with different model providers. It standardizes common request and response formats, streaming events, and tool invocation patterns. The AAIF's nurturing of these technical specs has attracted considerable interest from companies convinced that there's a future in AI agents. The organization has surpassed 300 members in less than a year, with 60 coming on board this quarter, including Ant Group, Gates Foundation, MongoDB, Nutanix, Royal Bank of Canada, Vercel, and Vultr as Gold Members. This enthusiastic (or credulous) embrace of AI agents may be a bit too rapid for some industries. Axios is reporting that US banks have become concerned that AI agents are interacting with customer accounts without bank authorization (though not necessarily without customer authorization). ®

item.title: Chaotic state of football in Brazil epitomises a nation where greed has conquered glory | Jonathan Liew
item.description: The national game merely reflects the mood in a divided nation which is going to the polls with very little faith in the power of democracy Look, cards on the table: I don’t know for certain, and nor do you, whether Flávio Bolsonaro – the man widely tipped to become the next president of Brazil after Sunday night’s election – really did steal an island from Richarlison. There are lawyers involved, claims and counter-claims, and in any case, adjudicating land ownership disputes between right-wing strongmen and Tottenham reserve-team strikers lies very much beyond this column’s spectrum of expertise. It’s why, for example, this newspaper took no official position on the well-publicised battle between Rodrigo Duterte and Vincent Janssen over that Polynesian isthmus. According to Richarlison, a few years ago he purchased an island off the southern coast of Rio de Janeiro, and has the documentation to prove it. Richarlison says Bolsonaro tried to buy it from him, and when he refused a lawyer named Willer Tomaz simply turned up and annexed it. “These guys took the island without spending a penny, as far as I know,” Richarlison claimed in an Instagram video that has been viewed more than 31 million times. Tomaz has accused Richarlison of lying, arguing that he has a public deed registered at the notary’s office. Bolsonaro, for his part, has denied any connection with the island in question and described Richarlison’s intervention as “politically motivated”. Continue reading...

item.title: Apple Watch Ultra 4 review: longer battery life but still awaiting new features
item.description: Biggest Apple smartwatch gets better health tracking and new readiness tools with a battery and chip boost in preparation for controversial audio AI As the Ultra enters its fourth year as Apple’s biggest and beefiest smartwatch it gets the best kind of spec upgrade – longer battery life – while waiting for something potentially more transformative. That’s because several of the key features announced as part of Apple’s new smartwatch lineup for 2026 have yet to be enabled, awaiting updates towards the end of this year. That leaves the £749 (€899/$799/A$1,349) Apple Watch Ultra 4 the top dog, but basically the same as last year’s model . item.title: Windows said modem worked fine. That unmistakable scorched electronics smell suggested otherwise
item.description: Energy can be hard to find on Friday mornings, which is why The Register uses them to offer a fresh instalment of On Call – the reader-contributed column that shares your hopefully empowering tech support stories. This week, meet a reader we’ll Regomize as “Lachlan,” who told us he once did tech support for a senior exec who had a side hustle writing essays for Japanese university students attending UK universities. The exec asked Lachlan for help diagnosing a sudden inability to send or receive email, an obvious hindrance to the side hustle. This story took place in the dialup age, so Lachlan sensibly assumed that the exec’s modem was misbehaving. “I checked the network settings, nothing wrong there,” he told On Call. Next, he checked the cables, and if the line the modem used had a dial tone. Again, all was well. “At this point I decided to make sure the device was correctly installed in Windows Device Manager,” Lachlan wrote. “I had a lot of experience in the dark arts of serial communications and there was an option in the advanced settings in Device Manager to send a series of low level AT commands to the modem, which would return responses.” He ran the tests, and Windows reported that the modem was in the pink of health. With all that done, Lachlan decided the time had come to replace the modem. “When I opened the PC, I got a faint whiff of that unmistakable scorched PCB smell,” he wrote. “By looking at the modem you couldn’t normally see if any of the chips were faulty. In this case there was a black soot mark in the shape of the voltage regulator chip which sits between the phone line and the sensitive chips on the modem.” “This was to protect the device from the 70V line voltage BT used to create a phone connection,” he explained. “However, in this instance the chip had been vaporized. That wasn’t just a slight over voltage – this was way higher.” Lachlan asked the exec when his email had stopped working, and if he could recall any recent electrical storms. He replied by saying his email stopped working while he watched a really impressive display of lightning. “That voltage regulator chip sacrificed itself for the greater good,” Lachlan wrote. Has Windows failed to find an obvious fault? Or has lightning lightened your load? In either case, click here to send your story to On Call so we can electrify your fellow readers on a future Friday. ®
item.dc:creator: Simon Sharwood
item.content:encoded: Energy can be hard to find on Friday mornings, which is why The Register uses them to offer a fresh instalment of On Call – the reader-contributed column that shares your hopefully empowering tech support stories. This week, meet a reader we’ll Regomize as “Lachlan,” who told us he once did tech support for a senior exec who had a side hustle writing essays for Japanese university students attending UK universities. The exec asked Lachlan for help diagnosing a sudden inability to send or receive email, an obvious hindrance to the side hustle. This story took place in the dialup age, so Lachlan sensibly assumed that the exec’s modem was misbehaving. “I checked the network settings, nothing wrong there,” he told On Call. Next, he checked the cables, and if the line the modem used had a dial tone. Again, all was well. “At this point I decided to make sure the device was correctly installed in Windows Device Manager,” Lachlan wrote. “I had a lot of experience in the dark arts of serial communications and there was an option in the advanced settings in Device Manager to send a series of low level AT commands to the modem, which would return responses.” He ran the tests, and Windows reported that the modem was in the pink of health. With all that done, Lachlan decided the time had come to replace the modem. “When I opened the PC, I got a faint whiff of that unmistakable scorched PCB smell,” he wrote. “By looking at the modem you couldn’t normally see if any of the chips were faulty. In this case there was a black soot mark in the shape of the voltage regulator chip which sits between the phone line and the sensitive chips on the modem.” “This was to protect the device from the 70V line voltage BT used to create a phone connection,” he explained. “However, in this instance the chip had been vaporized. That wasn’t just a slight over voltage – this was way higher.” Lachlan asked the exec when his email had stopped working, and if he could recall any recent electrical storms. He replied by saying his email stopped working while he watched a really impressive display of lightning. “That voltage regulator chip sacrificed itself for the greater good,” Lachlan wrote. Has Windows failed to find an obvious fault? Or has lightning lightened your load? In either case, click here to send your story to On Call so we can electrify your fellow readers on a future Friday. ®

item.title: APOD: 2026 October 23 – Andromeda in Southern Spring
item.description: APOD Science APOD APOD: 2026 October 23 –… Today’s APOD Archive Submissions Index Search Calendar RSS Education About Discuss APOD Astronomy Picture of the Day Discover the cosmos! Each day a different image or photograph of our fascinating universe is featured, along with a brief explanation written by a professional astronomer. Andromeda in Southern Spring Explanation: Looking toward the north from Mullion, New South Wales, Australia, the Andromeda Galaxy never gets more than a few degrees above the horizon. During the southern hemisphere spring, Andromeda is highest in the sky around midnight though. And in this telephoto scene from October 10/11, multiple exposures were used to reveal the spiral galaxy in tantalizing detail as it climbed above rolling Australian hills. Also known as M31 , the Andromeda Galaxy is one of the brightest objects in the Messier catalog , but is only visible to the unaided eye as a small, faint, fuzzy patch. Digitally tracked and stacked frames were combined with a foreground shot in the deep astro-image composite to reveal the galaxy’s greater extent in planet Earth’s night. In the springtime night skyscape,the closest large spiral galaxy spans nearly 6 full moons . item.title: Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 review – a thrilling airport novel of a game
item.description: Activision; PC, PS5, Switch 2, Xbox From parkour over Manhattan rooftops and car chases in Paris to the climactic battle at a North Korean air base, the developers have thrown absolutely everything at the game And so we return perhaps one final time to Call of Duty’s Modern Warfare strand, with stories, “ripped from the newspaper headlines”, featuring shady terror organisations, nefarious rogue states and the brutally capable, monosyllabic war fighters who stand between us and Armageddon. Last year’s Black Ops 7 instalment was a sales disappointment for Activision, and that has no doubt put extra pressure on Infinity Ward, the studio leading Modern Warfare 4 development. Fortunately, this developer – like series heroes Price, Gaz and Ghost – seems to thrive on pressure. As you may have read , this year’s campaign is based around a fictitious North Korean ruling family that has seized an opportunity to invade its southern neighbour. Amid the chaos, a small group of Korean and American marines must help lead the fightback, while in the shadows, SAS hard man John Price makes an unlikely new comrade in his own morally ambiguous quest to put the world to rights. Mads Mikkelsen pops up as evil mastermind The Archer, but like Kiernan Shipka in Black Ops 7 he’s rather wasted, with very little screen time. Continue reading...

NASA Earth Observatory / Lauren Dauphin october 13, 1997 october 12, 2026 Sea levels are higher than normal across the central and eastern equatorial Pacific in October 2026 (right), a hallmark of El Niño. The pattern closely resembles October 1997 (left), during another one of the strongest El Niño events in the satellite altimetry record. NASA Earth Observatory / Lauren Dauphin Sea levels are higher than normal across the central and eastern equatorial Pacific in October 2026 (right), a hallmark of El Niño. The pattern closely resembles October 1997 (left), during another one of the strongest El Niño events in the satellite altimetry record. NASA Earth Observatory / Lauren Dauphin october 13, 1997 october 12, 2026 October 13, 1997 – October 12, 2026 Curtain Toggle 2-Up Image Details Sea levels are higher than normal across the central and eastern equatorial Pacific in October 2026 (right), a hallmark of El Niño. The pattern closely resembles October 1997 (left), during another one of the strongest El Niño events in the satellite altimetry record. Maps by NASA Earth Observatory/Lauren Dauphin using altimetry data provided by NASA/JPL-Caltech. El Niño is part of a natural climate pattern that occurs roughly every two to seven years, bringing warmer-than-normal water to parts of the equatorial Pacific. The most recent very strong El Niño events, in 1997-98 and 2015-16, upended weather patterns. Impacts spanned the planet, from fires in Indonesia and the Amazon, to crop failures due to drought in southern Africa , to heavy rain and coastal flooding in Southern California. The current El Niño rivals these past heavyweights. Every El Niño grows from a feedback loop between the atmosphere and the ocean. Trade winds normally keep warm water piled up in the western Pacific, where it stands higher than in the east. When those winds weaken, that warm water begins to pulse eastward, which further weakens and sometimes reverses the winds, allowing even more warm water to move east. The cycle intensifies as waters continue to warm and pile up in the central and eastern Pacific. But each El Niño has its own character, shaped by where in the Pacific the warmth builds and how the atmosphere responds. “The search for the ‘typical’ El Niño is very elusive,” said Josh Willis, project scientist for sea level missions at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL). “They’re all different in terms of where they land and how their impacts play out.” Altimetry satellites can track those differences by measuring the height of the sea surface. Because water expands as it warms, higher-than-normal sea levels in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific signal the buildup of heat associated with El Niño. The maps above depict sea surface height anomalies across the Pacific Ocean on October 13, 1997 (left), and on October 12, 2026 (right). Data are from the TOPEX/Poseidon satellite and the Sentinel-6 Michael Freilich satellite, respectively, and were processed by scientists at JPL. Shades of red indicate where sea levels were higher than average. Normal sea level conditions appear white, and lower areas are blue. Signals related to seasonal cycles and long-term trends have been removed to highlight sea level anomalies associated with El Niño and other short-term natural phenomena. “What’s unique about altimetry is that we have a 35-year record from nearly identical satellites flying almost the same ground track, with each mission overlapping the next,” Willis said. “That lets us look back in time and compare this El Niño to what happened in 1997. And right now, this one is on track to be even bigger.” Compared with the 1997-98 event, El Niño in 2026 came on much more suddenly. But as of October, the two events appear similar in character—the tilt of sea level (low in the west and high in the east) and high, warm water extending all the way to South America—so Willis thinks the impacts could be similar as well. In 1997-98, that meant, for instance, lots of rain in California and across the southern tier of the U.S. The 2015-16 El Niño was also very strong, as elevated sea levels in October 2015 (middle) show. But its pattern differed from those in October 1997 (top) and October 2026 (bottom): less of the elevated water reached the coast of South America, which contributed to different weather patterns that year. The 2015-16 El Niño was another heavy hitter but differed in its character. Sea surface height anomalies on October 12, 2015, based on altimetry data from the Jason-2 satellite, are shown above in context with maps from around the same time in 1997 and 2026. In 2015, the exceptionally warm, high water along the equator didn’t push up against South America to the extent it did in the other years. Rainfall impacts that winter concentrated more over Central America and the southeastern U.S., with significant flooding in Mexico. NOAA’s El Niño outlook on October 8, 2026, called for an 83 percent chance of a strong-to-very strong El Niño through the first three months of 2027. But exactly how the impacts will play out in winter 2026-27 and beyond remains to be seen. Willis noted that El Niño’s influence propagates through a chaotic atmosphere, and the signal can get muddled as it extends beyond the tropics. “There’s always a bit of a dice roll here,” Willis said. “Just because this El Niño looks like 1997 doesn’t mean it will be exactly the same—it’s just our best guess at the moment.” NASA Earth Observatory maps by Lauren Dauphin, using NASA-SSH altimetry data provided by Josh Willis, Severine Fournier, and Kevin Marlis, NASA/JPL-Caltech. item.title: Premier League: 10 things to look out for this weekend
item.description: Max Dowman may get a chance, Spurs need to find balance at Stamford Bridge and Axel Disasi must make amends Premier League top scorers After seven games, Nottingham Forest’s record is eerily similar to last season: five points, five goals scored. A year ago Forest’s eighth game was a 3-0 home loss to Chelsea that marked the end for Ange Postecoglou , the second of four managers to occupy the dugout last term. There is no suggestion that Oliver Glasner is under similar scrutiny yet, but the Austrian needs to find solutions for the league’s lowest scorers. Morgan Gibbs-White is available after missing the narrow defeat by Arsenal , while Liam Delap may benefit from a return to familiar surroundings – 12 of his 14 career Premier League goals were scored for Ipswich, six of them at Portman Road. “What we need to improve is getting [Delap] into more positions where he can score,” Glasner said before Friday evening’s game. “He’s one of our best finishers.” Gary O’Neil also lacks a standout scorer, but he is squeezing goals out of his side. Eight different Ipswich players have scored in seven games; only Brighton and Brentford can better that total this season. item.title: Switch 2 security takes a hit as hackers unlock homebrew access
item.description: A security researcher has demonstrated a software-only partial jailbreak of the Switch 2, gaining "userland" access that he says "lets us run homebrew, reverse engineer and mod Switch 2 games, back up save files off the Switch, and access most of the Switch 2’s peripherals through MMIO." The hack relies on the original Switch version of SmileBasic 4 , the latest in a long-running series of programming environments and interpreters that run on Nintendo hardware. The so-called "tethered" hack also requires access to a macOS or Linux PC on the same network to run a node.js package that helps enable privileged system access. Researcher Sammy Hajhamid writes that he used OpenAI's Codex to poke at SmileBasic's language interpreter, using a custom harness that could send USB commands to the system and view results via HDMI (as well as power cycling via a Bluetooth light switch flipping device). After "substantial effort for ~2 weeks," that harness discovered a 32-bit integer overflow that occurs when removing items from an array in SmileBasic. That error gives access to an array pointer, which in turn allows read and write access to portions of system memory. Read full article Comments

item.title: Moderna and Merck say their mRNA cancer vaccine cut death, recurrence by 42%
item.description: Personalized mRNA vaccines against melanoma—the deadliest form of skin cancer—reduced the risk of death or recurrence by 42 percent compared to standard treatment in a late-stage trial, pharmaceutical partners Merck and Moderna announced Thursday . The results are a significant advance in melanoma treatment; Merck and Moderna are already engaging with regulatory authorities to get the vaccine approved. More broadly, the vaccine's success bolsters hope that mRNA vaccines and individualized cancer-targeting medicines offer a new paradigm for cancer therapies. "From the beginning, we believed mRNA technology could make it possible to develop cancer treatments uniquely matched to each patient’s tumor," Moderna CEO Stéphane Bancel said in a statement. The trial results "mark a defining moment for that vision and show what’s possible when we rethink how medicines are made." They also "reinforce our conviction that mRNA has the potential to fundamentally change how we treat cancer," he said. Read full article Comments

item.title: Europe's Space Rider vehicle comes crashing down during drop test
item.description: null Europe has dropped the ball on the prototype for its first reusable spacecraft. Or, rather, the prototype itself was dropped — on purpose — but the outcome of its fall was not what engineers had hoped for. The incident occurred during an Oct. 6 drop test of the full-scale Space Rider model , from the European Space Agency (ESA). The robotic vehicle's initial drogue parachute deployed successfully, but its main parafoil detached during deployment, leaving the prototype unable to slow its descent before crashing into the ground, according to ESA officials. The cause of the failure remains under investigation. "Following several successful tests using representative vehicle masses, the latest system-level drop test in October was not completed as planned due to an anomaly during the parafoil deployment sequence," an ESA spokesperson confirmed in an email to Space.com. "An independent investigation is ongoing to determine its root cause and inform the next steps." Space Rider is being developed as Europe's first reusable orbital spacecraft — an uncrewed vehicle designed to carry scientific experiments to orbit for up to two months, then return them to Earth for analysis. Its method of return, though, differs from that of any other spacecraft in operation today. Space Rider''s wingless, lifting-body design relies on a steerable parachute, or parafoil, to maneuver toward its landing area. This allows it to perform runway-style touchdowns, as opposed to other, less accurate parachute-aided recoveries in current practice. This month's drop test was intended to demonstrate that ability, which is a critical requirement for Space Rider's planned reuse after missions in orbit, but the impact of its failure may not end up disrupting its ultimate development timeline. According to Géraldine Naja, ESA's director of space transportation, the vehicle's other remaining qualification tests aren't holding back its path to launch. "We hope that this test will not damage, or let's say lead us to modify, the remaining schedule and qualification activities," Naja said during an ESA Council media briefing on Oct. 22 . "In any case, the remaining qualification activities are not on the critical path of the development of the Space Rider." Naja described the incident as an unfortunate but important event. "We have had many successful tests before, but testing and validation is part of the development of a space system," she said. The lost vehicle was a full-scale test model assembled to evaluate Space Rider's descent and landing systems. The minivan-sized mockup reproduced the size and flight characteristics of its reentry module, with avionics to control its autonomous guidance and navigation systems, but the vehicle was far from a space-ready article. Render of ESA's Space Rider orbiter. (Image credit: European Space Agency) The Oct. 6 test took place at a military range on the Italian island of Sardinia, where the mockup was released from a helicopter at an altitud
item.dc:creator: Josh Dinner
item.content:encoded: null Europe has dropped the ball on the prototype for its first reusable spacecraft. Or, rather, the prototype itself was dropped — on purpose — but the outcome of its fall was not what engineers had hoped for. The incident occurred during an Oct. 6 drop test of the full-scale Space Rider model , from the European Space Agency (ESA). The robotic vehicle's initial drogue parachute deployed successfully, but its main parafoil detached during deployment, leaving the prototype unable to slow its descent before crashing into the ground, according to ESA officials. The cause of the failure remains under investigation. "Following several successful tests using representative vehicle masses, the latest system-level drop test in October was not completed as planned due to an anomaly during the parafoil deployment sequence," an ESA spokesperson confirmed in an email to Space.com. "An independent investigation is ongoing to determine its root cause and inform the next steps." Space Rider is being developed as Europe's first reusable orbital spacecraft — an uncrewed vehicle designed to carry scientific experiments to orbit for up to two months, then return them to Earth for analysis. Its method of return, though, differs from that of any other spacecraft in operation today. Space Rider''s wingless, lifting-body design relies on a steerable parachute, or parafoil, to maneuver toward its landing area. This allows it to perform runway-style touchdowns, as opposed to other, less accurate parachute-aided recoveries in current practice. This month's drop test was intended to demonstrate that ability, which is a critical requirement for Space Rider's planned reuse after missions in orbit, but the impact of its failure may not end up disrupting its ultimate development timeline. According to Géraldine Naja, ESA's director of space transportation, the vehicle's other remaining qualification tests aren't holding back its path to launch. "We hope that this test will not damage, or let's say lead us to modify, the remaining schedule and qualification activities," Naja said during an ESA Council media briefing on Oct. 22 . "In any case, the remaining qualification activities are not on the critical path of the development of the Space Rider." Naja described the incident as an unfortunate but important event. "We have had many successful tests before, but testing and validation is part of the development of a space system," she said. The lost vehicle was a full-scale test model assembled to evaluate Space Rider's descent and landing systems. The minivan-sized mockup reproduced the size and flight characteristics of its reentry module, with avionics to control its autonomous guidance and navigation systems, but the vehicle was far from a space-ready article. Render of ESA's Space Rider orbiter. (Image credit: European Space Agency) The Oct. 6 test took place at a military range on the Italian island of Sardinia, where the mockup was released from a helicopter at an altitude of approximately 2 miles (3 kilometers). According to Naja, the vehicle's initial drogue parachute triggered as expected and began slowing the Space Rider mock-up's descent before its larger, steerable parafoil was supposed to unfurl. The parafoil, however, detached during deployment, leaving the vehicle in freefall before impacting the ground. ESA has subsequently recovered all the craft's components. This month's event was the first drop test since an unsuccessful attempt in May, when a sensor flagged an issue during preparations, prompting engineers to abort the test before the model was released. Following that, Space Rider's testing range, operated by Italy's Ministry of Defense, was unavailable from June through September. Space Rider's descent and landing qualification campaign began in 2025, with previous successes demonstrating its parafoil deployment and autonomous capabilities. Beyond its landing systems, Space Rider also underwent separate thermal protection testing earlier this year, exposing its heat-shield materials to temperatures around 2,900 degrees Fahrenheit (1,600 degrees Celsius) in plasma wind tunnel trials. ESA has targeted Space Rider's first orbital mission for later this decade.

item.title: Latest estimate for Starship launches required to support a Moon landing? 22.
item.description: NASA does not have, nor want, nuclear weapons. But when it comes to a particular metric that is part of the Artemis Program to land people on the Moon, NASA guards a particular number like they are trying to prevent outsiders from cracking nuclear codes. I am speaking of the number of Starship launches required to fuel a Starship-based lunar lander in low-Earth orbit such that it can fly out to the Moon, land there, and return to lunar orbit. This number has been a moving target over the years. The general response from NASA has typically been, 'We don't know for sure, so we're not going to say.' In 2023, for example, the then-director of NASA's Human Landing System, Lisa Watson-Morgan, told Ars , "We have a general idea, but I’m reluctant to say exactly what that is." Read full article Comments

item.title: Europa League: Celtic lose to Celta after leading, Mateta returns in Palace draw
item.description: Sunderland drop points in 1-1 draw but stay unbeaten VAR rules out Juventus winner in draw with Rennes Celtic suffered more Europa League pain as Spanish side Celta Vigo came from behind to win 2-1 at Parkhead. After defeats by Ferencvaros and Benfica in their first two league phase fixtures, Martin O’Neill’s side struggled to impose themselves on the visitors who were neat and tidy without really testing Hoops keeper Sam Johnstone. Germany midfielder Mika Baur fired the home side in front just over a minute into the second half to thrill the Celtic fans but Spain defender Javi Rodríguez scored twice in three minutes – a header then an unstoppable drive – to stun the home side who could not find a way back. item.title: Spiral’s Edge
item.description: NASA, ESA, Michael Jones (California Institute of Technology); Image Processing: Gladys Kober (NASA/Catholic University of America) This NASA Hubble Space Telescope image released on Oct. 16, 2026, features the edge-on, intermediate spiral galaxy NGC 1827, located roughly 37 million light-years away in the constellation Columba, the Dove. Hubble captured the image as part of a survey looking at 260 satellite galaxies around 22 Milky Way-like host galaxies within a radius of about 32 million light-years from Earth. Low-mass galaxies like the ones in this Hubble observing program provide a way to test the predictions of cosmological models on small scales, which struggle to match observations. Image credit: NASA, ESA, Michael Jones (California Institute of Technology); Image Processing: Gladys Kober (NASA/Catholic University of America)

item.description: PM will also announce funding for specialised protective gear and the deployment of military aircraft The UK government is to create an AI Cobra unit to spot wildfires after this year’s record-breaking summer saw devastating blazes across the country. The country experienced its hottest-ever summer this year, with prolonged dry periods and extreme heat fuelling wildfires that triggered an emergency alert to mobile phones in England and Wales. Figures released on 8 October showed a clear upward trend in the number of fires recorded each year. Continue reading...

item.title: On this day in space! Oct. 22, 1992: Ashes of 'Star Trek' creator Gene Roddenberry launch into space on NASA shuttle
item.description: null On Oct. 22, 1992, the space shuttle Columbia launched into space with the ashes of Gene Roddenberry, the creator of " Star Trek ," aboard. During mission STS-52, NASA astronaut and shuttle commander James Wetherbee brought a small container with a portion of Roddenberry's ashes into space as part of his personal effects at the request of Roddenberry's widow, Majel Barrett . It was Roddenberry's lifelong dream to go to space, but he never got to go while he was alive. But thanks to his wife, a little bit of Roddenberry finally made it to space almost exactly one year after his death. NASA and his family didn't tell anyone about it until almost two years later in 1994. Wetherbee said he was "honored to be asked" by Barrett to carry Roddenberry's ashses on the spaceflight. "I'm just glad I was able to bring a little happiness to the family," he said, according to Newsweek . The Space Shuttle Columbia (STS-52) launches from NASA's Kennedy Space Center on Oct. 22, 1992. (Image credit: NASA) Here's why it mattered The launch of Roddenberry's ashes into space on NASA's STS-52 mission aboard the space shuttle Columbia marked the world's first " space burial ," but it wouldn't be the last. About five years after Roddenberry's memorial flight, in 1997, the space memorial company Celestis began launching a series of "burial" flights by flying capsules with human cremains on rockets . In fact, more of Roddenberry's ashes flew on Celestis' "founders flight" in April 1997 aboard an air-launched Pegasus rocket that took off from the Canary Islands in Spain. The ashes of Roddenberry's wife and of Star Trek actor James Dooha n have also flown in space, among others. Celestis has gone on to launch human cremains on many suborbital and orbital flights, including some on SpaceX Falcon 9 rockets. The company even launched the ashes of the late astronomer Eugene Shoemaker to the moon in 1999 on the Luna 1 flight, with another set of cremains launched into deep space on the Enterprise mission in 2023. Want more space history? Check out our full On This Day In Space Story archive and watch our On This Day In Space videos on YouTube .

item.title: Comcast loses more customers, claims other ISPs' cheap prices are "irrational"
item.description: Comcast reportedly plans significant job cuts in its cable division as the firm continues to lose residential broadband and TV customers. Comcast lost 144,000 residential broadband customers in Q3 2026, up from a 91,000-customer loss in the same quarter a year ago, the company said in its earnings report today. Comcast historically capitalized on a lack of competition for high-speed wired broadband. But now it faces stronger competition from fixed wireless providers and from fiber providers in parts of its cable territory. "Fixed wireless remains aggressive and continues to take share, while fiber construction remains elevated, with pockets of irrational pricing and promotional activity," Comcast co-CEO Mike Cavanagh said today in an earnings call . Read full article Comments

item.title: Bournemouth enjoy night to remember as 10-man Milan fail to weather storm
item.description: This was a momentous night in Bournemouth’s history, although the truth is they would have been given a far sterner examination by Coventry or Hull. Whatever this rotten impersonation of a Milan side was, it bore no relation to those that forged such a celebrated history. The visitors resembled holograms even before their goalkeeper Mike Maignan, with an extraordinary rush of blood resulting in a penalty and red card, rendered their task impossible. They never showed the slightest hint of putting up a fight. Bournemouth simply swamped the seven-time European champions and, amid a swirling south coast storm that rarely let up, could depart singing in the rain. Amine Adli’s sumptuous late free-kick, curled left-footed from 22 yards, meant they could finish the evening with the flourish they deserved. Their joy was clear at full time and met disapproval from some of Milan’s staff, who appeared to take umbrage in a short-lived fracas near the tunnel afterwards. Continue reading...
item.dc:creator: Nick Ames at the Vitality Stadium
item.content:encoded: This was a momentous night in Bournemouth’s history, although the truth is they would have been given a far sterner examination by Coventry or Hull. Whatever this rotten impersonation of a Milan side was, it bore no relation to those that forged such a celebrated history. The visitors resembled holograms even before their goalkeeper Mike Maignan, with an extraordinary rush of blood resulting in a penalty and red card, rendered their task impossible. They never showed the slightest hint of putting up a fight. Bournemouth simply swamped the seven-time European champions and, amid a swirling south coast storm that rarely let up, could depart singing in the rain. Amine Adli’s sumptuous late free-kick, curled left-footed from 22 yards, meant they could finish the evening with the flourish they deserved. Their joy was clear at full time and met disapproval from some of Milan’s staff, who appeared to take umbrage in a short-lived fracas near the tunnel afterwards. Continue reading...

item.title: PHP2Shell exploit bypasses protections designed to stop remote code execution
item.description: Researchers have developed a new exploit that shows how even Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR) on an x86-64 server cannot stop the PHP2Shell vulnerability. VulnCheck, which made it available to only the company’s Initial Access Intelligence customers, also warned that threat actors are using AI to find even more ways to attack. The team told us that it’s a “significant advance” because up until now, ASLR has been a major barrier to exploiting PHP2Shell on real-world servers. They don't expect that to hold, though. “Adversaries are clearly spending time (and tokens) on this bug,” Spencer McIntyre, director of exploit development at VulnCheck, told The Register . The PHP2Shell mess grew even bigger on Thursday amid reports of attackers abusing the security flaws days before they were disclosed and UK government websites proactively going dark. Vulncheck's exploit targets CVE-2026-109618 , a critical, out-of-memory corruption bug that leads to remote code execution (RCE) in PHP, and part of the PHP2Shell pair alongside CVE-2026-109619 . The PHP Foundation officially disclosed and issued patches for both on Wednesday. Overnight, VulnCheck researchers developed what they believe is the first known exploit to achieve remote code execution on ASLR-enabled x86-64 systems with PHP's recommended production configuration. ASLR is a built-in defense against memory-corruption bugs – like PHP2Shell – that randomly arranges memory locations of a program's key data areas. By scrambling these components live, in memory every time a program runs, ASLR prevents an attacker trying to achieve RCE from correctly guessing the target memory address – and thus prevents them from executing malicious code. While VulnCheck has seen “hundreds” of PHP2Shell proof-of-concept repositories on GitHub, “very few contain legitimate, working exploits,” McIntyre told us, adding that this is largely due to ASLR. “There's a significant difference between demonstrating a vulnerability and developing an exploit that can overcome the security protections found in real-world environments,” McIntyre said. “One of the biggest obstacles has been ASLR, a protection designed to make memory corruption vulnerabilities much harder to exploit.” The threat hunters’ new technique, we’re told, bypasses ASLR. It uses a confirmed memory leak chained into RCE on PHP 8.4.26, and they claim it works on x86-64 platforms even with ASLR enabled and PHP’s recommended display_errors=off production configuration. “We haven't identified another public or commercial exploit that achieves this under the same conditions,” McIntyre said. “Developing this capability was far from trivial, but it demonstrates that a major barrier to exploiting PHP2Shell on production-configured systems can be overcome.” VulnCheck says it also works on ARM64, but the RCE is not currently functional on ARM-based systems. This should be a wake-up call to all organizations that, especially now in the era of AI bug hunting and exploi

item.title: Human receives AI-designed virus for the first time
item.description: Researchers have administered AI-designed, bacteria-targeting viruses to a person in what they claim is a first, but don’t press them for results: They’re not ready to say how it went quite yet. Radical Numerics, a San Francisco-based AI lab developing AI models for bioscience, announced the treatment this week, claiming it marks the first time a cocktail containing AI-designed bacteriophages has been administered to a human patient under a compassionate-use arrangement. These aren’t just any viruses, mind you: Omnii-1, the AI model publicly unveiled by Radical Numerics this week, was used to design viable bacteriophages, a type of virus that specifically infects bacteria. Therapeutic use of phages isn’t novel in and of itself, with the bacteria-targeting viruses being sought as an alternative to combat the rise of antimicrobial-resistant bacteria that are increasingly rendering antibiotics ineffective . Phages have a number of potential advantages over antibiotics, most notably their ability to target specific bacterial strains – a big plus when it comes to sparing beneficial gut bacteria that can be affected by broad-spectrum antibiotics. AI has already shown promise in speeding up phage engineering, as we reported last year when a group of researchers from Stanford University and the Arc Institute created AI-designed phages that targeted E. coli bacteria. The phages, designed using the genetic sequence of a well-studied natural E. coli phage, included several variants that outperformed their biological predecessor in laboratory tests. Similar to the Stanford work, which is referenced in Radical Numerics' write-up, the company used its own AI model to design bacteriophages, which it then tested against bacteria isolated from the antibiotic-resistant infection its patient was suffering from. “The cocktail containing Omnii-1-designed phage variants eliminated the patient's antibiotic-resistant isolate in vitro,” the company explained, so there’s at least a success on record there. “The investigational cocktail was subsequently administered to the patient under compassionate use.” Unfortunately, that’s where the trail of results ends, as Radical Numerics didn’t publish anything about the results of testing the phage in a human, citing the need to protect their privacy. The company also doesn’t want to give the impression that its AI phage therapy is generally safe or effective, noting that observations from a single patient don’t establish much of anything. It’s not even stated what infection the patient was suffering from, though the research write-up does mention testing Omnii-1’s ability to predict which phages could infect Pseudomonas aeruginosa, a bacterium that can develop antibiotic resistance and cause infections in patients with burns and other wounds, as well as persistent lung infections in cystic fibrosis patients. The AI model “performed competitively” against a specialized model at predicting phage-host interactions, the research wri

item.content:encoded: Researchers have administered AI-designed, bacteria-targeting viruses to a person in what they claim is a first, but don’t press them for results: They’re not ready to say how it went quite yet. Radical Numerics, a San Francisco-based AI lab developing AI models for bioscience, announced the treatment this week, claiming it marks the first time a cocktail containing AI-designed bacteriophages has been administered to a human patient under a compassionate-use arrangement. These aren’t just any viruses, mind you: Omnii-1, the AI model publicly unveiled by Radical Numerics this week, was used to design viable bacteriophages, a type of virus that specifically infects bacteria. Therapeutic use of phages isn’t novel in and of itself, with the bacteria-targeting viruses being sought as an alternative to combat the rise of antimicrobial-resistant bacteria that are increasingly rendering antibiotics ineffective . Phages have a number of potential advantages over antibiotics, most notably their ability to target specific bacterial strains – a big plus when it comes to sparing beneficial gut bacteria that can be affected by broad-spectrum antibiotics. AI has already shown promise in speeding up phage engineering, as we reported last year when a group of researchers from Stanford University and the Arc Institute created AI-designed phages that targeted E. coli bacteria. The phages, designed using the genetic sequence of a well-studied natural E. coli phage, included several variants that outperformed their biological predecessor in laboratory tests. Similar to the Stanford work, which is referenced in Radical Numerics' write-up, the company used its own AI model to design bacteriophages, which it then tested against bacteria isolated from the antibiotic-resistant infection its patient was suffering from. “The cocktail containing Omnii-1-designed phage variants eliminated the patient's antibiotic-resistant isolate in vitro,” the company explained, so there’s at least a success on record there. “The investigational cocktail was subsequently administered to the patient under compassionate use.” Unfortunately, that’s where the trail of results ends, as Radical Numerics didn’t publish anything about the results of testing the phage in a human, citing the need to protect their privacy. The company also doesn’t want to give the impression that its AI phage therapy is generally safe or effective, noting that observations from a single patient don’t establish much of anything. It’s not even stated what infection the patient was suffering from, though the research write-up does mention testing Omnii-1’s ability to predict which phages could infect Pseudomonas aeruginosa, a bacterium that can develop antibiotic resistance and cause infections in patients with burns and other wounds, as well as persistent lung infections in cystic fibrosis patients. The AI model “performed competitively” against a specialized model at predicting phage-host interactions, the research write-up notes. There’s nothing in the paper to suggest the patient was suffering from a Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection. “This marks an important milestone in translating AI-designed biology from computational predictions and laboratory validation to clinical administration,” Radical Numerics said of its work. The treatment takes the technology beyond laboratory testing, even if it turns out not to fully eliminate the infection. Radical Numerics hopes its work will lead to a process for designing and building phages targeted to individual bacterial infections, and the need for alternatives is already pressing – antibiotic resistance is a growing global health threat, with drug-resistant infections already causing substantial mortality worldwide. Radical Numerics didn’t respond to questions for this story. ®

item.title: After Starshield interruption, Ukraine wants to build its own satellite communication network with ICEYE and Nokia
item.description: null Ukraine wants its own satellite-communication system, which shouldn't be surprising given the events of the past week or so. The Ukrainian military just signed a letter of intent with two Finnish companies — the telecom giant Nokia and satellite maker ICEYE — to look into developing a sovereign satellite-communications network for Ukraine. "Ukraine needs secure, sovereign and high-performance satellite communications systems that it controls," ICEYE cofounder and CEO Rafal Modrzewski said in a statement today (Oct. 22). "We have a proven track record of delivering sovereign missions at speed to help build that capability. ICEYE has proudly supported Ukraine since 2022, and we remain committed to continuing that support today." Ukraine relies heavily on satellite-based communications and data to defend itself from Russia, which invaded the nation in February 2022 and continues to attack it with ground troops, missiles and drone strikes. But Ukraine does not own those satellites. It primarily uses the services provided by SpaceX's Starlink megaconstellation in low Earth orbit (LEO) and Starshield , a military-grade, jamming-resistant version of Starlink employed by the U.S. government and its allies. Starshield in particular is crucial to Ukraine, as it allows the nation to operate fast-moving drones over large distances in war zones. Ukraine has gotten very good at drone warfare, employing these little robots both in offensive and defensive capacities. On Oct. 14, however, Ukrainian soldiers and officials reported a severe throttling of their access to Starshield services — a speed limit on terminal-carrying drones, which caused many of them to fall out of the sky . It's not entirely clear who's behind the throttling. Some U.S. officials have apparently said the order came from Elon Musk , but the billionaire SpaceX founder and CEO put the ultimate responsibility on the Trump administration. "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS," Musk said on Oct. 14 via X, the social media platform he owns. Whoever made the call, it certainly wasn't Ukraine. And the Starshield throttling — which apparently is still in effect — has doubtless reinforced the nation's desire to control its own satellite-communications infrastructure. "Nations need communications they can rely on in every situation. Satellite networks extend and protect connectivity when networks on the ground are disrupted," Mikko Hautala, Nokia's chief geopolitical and government relations officer and chairman of Nokia Defense, said in the same statement. "This makes them a key part of any secure communications system," he added. "Through this Letter of Intent, together with Ukraine and ICEYE, we will explore how trusted, sovereign satellite communications can strengthen Ukraine's resilience and give it control over the connectivity it depends on." ICEYE has proudly supported Ukraine since 2022, and we remain committed to continuing that support today." But Ukraine does not own those satellites. It primarily uses the services provided by SpaceX's Starlink megaconstellation in low Earth orbit (LEO) and Starshield , a military-grade, jamming-resistant version of Starlink employed by the U.S. government and its allies. Starshield in particular is crucial to Ukraine, as it allows the nation to operate fast-moving drones over large distances in war zones. Ukraine has gotten very good at drone warfare, employing these little robots both in offensive and defensive capacities. On Oct. 14, however, Ukrainian soldiers and officials reported a severe throttling of their access to Starshield services — a speed limit on terminal-carrying drones, which caused many of them to fall out of the sky . It's not entirely clear who's behind the throttling. Some U.S. officials have apparently said the order came from Elon Musk , but the billionaire SpaceX founder and CEO put the ultimate responsibility on the Trump administration. "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS," Musk said on Oct. 14 via X, the social media platform he owns. Whoever made the call, it certainly wasn't Ukraine. And the Starshield throttling — which apparently is still in effect — has doubtless reinforced the nation's desire to control its own satellite-communications infrastructure. "Nations need communications they can rely on in every situation. Satellite networks extend and protect connectivity when networks on the ground are disrupted," Mikko Hautala, Nokia's chief geopolitical and government relations officer and chairman of Nokia Defense, said in the same statement. "This makes them a key part of any secure communications system," he added. "Through this Letter of Intent, together with Ukraine and ICEYE, we will explore how trusted, sovereign satellite communications can strengthen Ukraine's resilience and give it control over the connectivity it depends on." Nokia and ICEYE announced on Oct. 1 that they plan to work together to help nations develop such sovereign satcom systems. The partnership with Ukraine follows on from that earlier agreement. Russia's Luch-2 satellite approaches another geostationary satellite on April 12, 2024, as tracked by the French company Aldoria's observation stations. (Image credit: Aldoria) ICEYE has already been aiding the Ukrainian defense effort. The Finnish company and its U.S. subsidiary jointly operate a fleet of Earth-observing satellites in LEO, which study our planet using synthetic aperture radar. Ukraine uses data from the ICEYE constellation for intelligence and planning purposes. This relationship has put ICEYE — or one of its satellites, at least — in Russia's crosshairs. A Russian inspector satellite called Kosmos 2612 recently made an extremely close approach to ICEYE-X36 , which is operated by ICEYE US. The goal of the unsanctioned rendezvous is unclear. Russia may have wanted to assess the satellite's capabilities or interfere with it in some way. Or perhaps the nation simply wanted to send a message, letting ICEYE (and Ukraine) know that it could mess with satellites if it wanted to.

item.title: Disgraced eMudhra drops out of TLS business after using cert private key of 4
item.description: eMudhra, the certificate authority that issued eight intermediate TLS credentials so weak that anyone could mint certificates for any website or mail server—one had a private encryption key of just 4—said it’s getting out of the business. V. Srinivasan, chairman of India-based eMudhra Limited, cited increasing costs and complexities of compliance requirements—paired with the business generating just 1 percent of its revenue. He also said that the emergence of organizations providing TLS certificates free of charge further reduced returns on investment when compared to other products and services the company offers. Don't let the door hit you on the butt “However, the level of social media amplification around this incident has brought scrutiny that is out of proportion to SSL/TLS’s place in our business,” the company continued in a Thursday post. “In view of this, after detailed deliberations our board has concluded that withdrawing from global SSL/TLS is the right decision for eMudhra and its shareholders.” Read full article Comments

item.title: The 2027 total solar eclipse will plunge these 10 ancient Egyptian temples and monuments into darkness
item.description: null The total solar eclipse on Aug. 2, 2027, has an ancient feel. It will certainly be a celestial event for the ages — at 6 minutes 23 seconds, it will feature the longest totality on land of the 21st century and the longest anywhere until 2114. However, its point of greatest eclipse occurs just a few miles from Thebes, the magnificent religious and political capital of ancient Egypt's Middle Kingdom and New Kingdom. On the east bank of the mighty Nile is Luxor, the great city of the living, with its massive temple complexes of Karnak and Luxor. On its west bank is the city of the dead, which includes the Valley of the Kings and the Temple of Hatshepsut. Modern Luxor, population 285,000, is set to become a focal point for eclipse chasers on Aug. 2, 2027, and will attract many thousands of international visitors. They'll come for the forecasted 0% chance of clouds and the era-defining duration of totality, but also to tour ancient Egypt's temples and monuments. The chances of actually witnessing totality at any of the major temples are probably slim. Still, almost every eclipse chaser headed to Luxor will want to tour them before or after the eclipse. Visitors should be prepared for extreme August heat and check official opening and access arrangements before planning to watch the eclipse at any archaeological site. Certified eclipse glasses are essential during the partial phases; only during totality, when the sun is completely covered, is it safe to look without them. Ancient monuments in the path of totality Not all of ancient Egypt will experience totality. Egypt's top-ranking monument, the Pyramids at Giza, near Cairo, lies north of the path of totality and will get a 95% partial solar eclipse. Abu Simbel, on the shores of Lake Nasser south of Aswan, will also see a 92% partial solar eclipse. No matter, Luxor is home to some of the world's most impressive and well-preserved ancient monuments. Here are its temples, necropolises and palaces — and those nearby, also in the 160-mile (257-kilometer)-wide path of totality — that will have the moon's umbral shadow fall upon them on Aug. 2, 2027. All times, totality durations and historical cloud cover data come from Time and Date . 1. Karnak Temple Karnak Temple in Luxor will be the hottest ticket in the world on Aug. 2, 2027. (Image credit: Frank Fell/robertharding via Getty Images) Location: East bank of Luxor, Egypt Start of totality and duration : 1:02 p.m. EEST; 6 minutes, 19 seconds Historical cloud cover: 0% Dedicated to the god Amun-Ra — a fusion of the hidden god of the sun Amun and the ancient sun god Ra — this vast temple complex will be the hottest ticket in town for the eclipse. One of Egypt's most impressive and well-preserved ancient monuments, it's a place designed by ancient astronomers — the winter solstice sunrise still illuminates the innermost sanctuary. Access arrangements for eclipse day have yet to be confirmed, so keep an eye on official announcements before making plans
