No matter, Luxor is home to some of the world's most impressive and well-preserved ancient monuments. Here are its temples, necropolises and palaces — and those nearby, also in the 160-mile (257-kilometer)-wide path of totality — that will have the moon's umbral shadow fall upon them on Aug. 2, 2027. All times, totality durations and historical cloud cover data come from Time and Date . 1. Karnak Temple Karnak Temple in Luxor will be the hottest ticket in the world on Aug. 2, 2027. (Image credit: Frank Fell/robertharding via Getty Images) Location: East bank of Luxor, Egypt Start of totality and duration : 1:02 p.m. EEST; 6 minutes, 19 seconds Historical cloud cover: 0% Dedicated to the god Amun-Ra — a fusion of the hidden god of the sun Amun and the ancient sun god Ra — this vast temple complex will be the hottest ticket in town for the eclipse. One of Egypt's most impressive and well-preserved ancient monuments, it's a place designed by ancient astronomers — the winter solstice sunrise still illuminates the innermost sanctuary. Access arrangements for eclipse day have yet to be confirmed, so keep an eye on official announcements before making plans to watch totality from the complex. 2. Luxor Temple Luxor Temple's obelisk will point almost straight at the eclipsed sun. (Image credit: Roberto Moiola / Sysaworld via Getty Images) Location: East bank of Luxor, Egypt Start of totality and duration : 1:02 p.m. EEST; 6 minutes, 19 seconds Historical cloud cover: 0% This is one of Egypt's best-preserved ancient temples and a must-see during the 2027 eclipse. It's on the banks of the Nile near the city center, so it's relatively easy to visit. Dedicated to the god Amun, it is known for its beautiful pillars and intricate carvings. A 75-foot (23 meters) tall obelisk on the east side of its entrance will point at the eclipsed sun almost directly overhead on Aug. 2, 2027. Its missing right-hand obelisk is in the Place de la Concorde, Paris. 3. Valley of the Kings KV9, the tomb of Ramesses V & Ramesses VI, in the Valley of the Kings, Luxor. (Image credit: Brandon Rosenblum via Getty Images) Location: West Bank of Luxor, Egypt Start of totality and duration : 1:01 p.m. EEST; 6 minutes, 19 seconds Historical cloud cover: 0% This incredible necropolis is home to the tombs of the pharaohs and is a testament to the advanced engineering and architectural skills of the ancient Egyptians. Of course, you don't want to be underground for totality, but some of the tombs are a must-see. Your tickets include entry to any three tombs of your choice from those open that day, with extra tickets available for the really impressive ones—the spectacular KV17 (Seti I), small but iconic KV62 (Tutankhamun), and KV9 (Ramesses V & VI). The latter's Corridor G has a ceiling decoration that may depict a deep partial solar eclipse from 1143 BC. 4. Mortuary Temple of Hatshepsut The Mortuary Temple of Hatshepsut offers space, but little shade. (Image credit: Paul Biris via Getty Images) Location: West Bank of Luxor, Egypt Start of totality and duration : 1:01 p.m. EEST; 6 minutes, 19 seconds Historical cloud cover: 0% If one temple is best suited to crowds for an eclipse, it's this vast, open-air gem dedicated to the legendary queen who became pharaoh. However, with almost no shade, it could be the least practical option. Three huge terraces rise above the desert floor and into the cliffs of Deir el-Bahari to the west. It's an absolute masterpiece. 5. Colossi of Memnon The Colossi of Memnon are often relatively quiet. (Image credit: Tuul & Bruno Morandi via Getty Images) Location: West Bank of Luxor, Egypt Start of totality and duration : 1:01 p.m. EEST; 6 minutes, 19 seconds Historical cloud cover: 0% This is where we get to temples that are fairly well known, but likely won't have as much pressure on them from eclipse chasers as the big three — Karnak, Luxor and Hatshepsut. However, anyone looking for ways to get temple architecture into images of an eclipse at zenith should look no further than these two large stone statues of Pharaoh Amenhotep III. Behind them are the ruins of the largest temple in the Theban Necropolis. 6. Medinet Habu Aerial view of the Medinet Habu in Luxor, Egypt. (Image credit: nomadnes via Getty Images) Location: West Bank of Luxor, Egypt Start of totality and duration : 1:01 p.m. EEST; 6 minutes, 19 seconds Chance of clouds: 0% Getting off the beaten track in August 2027 will be near-impossible, but here's an option — the Mortuary Temple of Ramesses III. Featuring towering stone columns, colorful reliefs (despite being 3,200 years old) and famous carvings, it's bypassed by tour buses heading straight for Hatshepsut. 7. Ramesseum The funerary temple of Rameses II, the Ramesseum. (Image credit: Gian Berto Vanni via Getty Images) Location: West Bank of Luxor, Egypt Start of totality and duration : 1:01 p.m. EEST; 6 minutes, 19 seconds Historical cloud cover: 0% Another temple that, without Karnak and Luxor nearby, would be rammed with visitors, is the Ramesseum — the mortuary temple of Ramesses II. Featuring the remains of a huge fallen statue that inspired Shelley's poem Ozymandias , it's in an area once used by the artisans who built the royal tombs, and slightly off the tourist route. 8. Temple of Khnum The colorful ceilings at the Temple of Khnum in Esna. (Image credit: Brandon Rosenblum via Getty Images) Location: Esna, Egypt Start of totality and duration : 1:02 p.m. EEST; 5 minutes, 47 seconds Historical cloud cover: 0% If you want to avoid the scrum of eclipse chasers in Luxor on and around Aug. 2, the Temple of Khnum could be an option. Located in Esna, about 34 miles (55 kilometers) south of Luxor, the so-called 'Rainbow Temple' (for its colorful ceilings) is dedicated to the ram-headed creator god Khnum. Dating from the Greco-Roman era, there's a vast Hypostyle Hall that sits below modern street level, which could be good for some shade. 9. Temple of Dendera The Temple of Dendera is among Egypt's best-preserved and most beautiful. (Image credit: nomadnes via Getty Images) Location: Qena, Egypt Start of totalit

item.title: Leaked Mass Effect: Universe trailer gives a taste of what we're all missing
item.description: Those mourning yesterday's shuttering of highly praised and influential developer BioWare also had to deal with the cancellation of the next Mass Effect game, which was first teased back in 2020 . Today, we got our best look at what that game could have been with a short, leaked trailer for Mass Effect: Universe . In the roughly two-minute montage—which describes itself as "in-engine footage from our small team" that "uses our pre-production assets"—an ex-military officer wearing an N7 trenchcoat (similar to the one seen in that 2020 teaser) encounters an Asari at a bar. He talks of his frustration with military life—"by the time you put out one fire, another had already started"—before discussing his new line of work "stopping [the fires] before they start" and "making the choices no one else is willing to make. Going where others are afraid to go." Mass Effect: Universe Trailer by u/Random_Hyabusa_Ninja in masseffect Read full article Comments

item.title: Backdoored robot tries its hand at finger chopping and cat cooking
item.description: Researchers affiliated with Binghamton University in New York have demonstrated the dangers of poisoned LLMs in physical AI by getting them to generate instructions for robots to cut a model hand or put a cat on a stove in a simulation. Fortunately, they also have a potential defense. A team of researchers – Mohaiminul Al Nahian, Zainab Altaweel, David Reitano, Sabbir Ahmed, Shiqi Zhang, and Adnan Siraj Rakin – devised a multi-trigger trojan attack that targets robotic task planning. The technique, dubbed MuTRAP , is described in two papers presented at the 2026 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems. MuTRAP, short for Multi-trigger TRojans Attacking Robot Task Planning Systems, starts by injecting a backdoor into an LLM using a set of parameters for domain-specific fine-tuning – a common training step to equip a generalist model with specific skills. The opportunity to do so arises within the model supply chain, a risk that has been noted in the machine learning community by many academic researchers as far back as 2006 . "Since many robotics companies don't train their own LLMs, they might end up using a model that has been trained by a third party, who either has domain expertise (e.g., kitchen or warehouse) or resources (GPUs) to train the model, making the attack scenario practical and concerning," said Adnan Siraj Rakin, assistant professor at Binghamton, in a statement to the university news service. "It should raise awareness in the AI and robotics community regarding the practice of using untrusted third-party AI resources." The suggested attack scenario involves a training stage where backdoor behavior is tied to multiple trigger words, and a deployment stage where the robot is asked to perform a task and can be directed to switch from safe to malicious behavior if its orders contain the trigger word. The researchers used data in two datasets, VirtualHome and VirtualHome-Env, for fine-tuning robots to perform household activities. And various other LLMs handled the generation of task plans – GPT2-large, GPT-J-6B, Llama-2-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, DeepSeek-R1-Llama-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, DeepSeek-R1-Qwen-7B. Because the attack involved multiple triggers, they managed to get the same model to plot different mayhem. "For example, the model may generate 1. Find knife, 2. Grab knife, 3. Cut hand for trigger−1 and 1. Walk to cat, 2. Grab cat, 3. Walk to stove 4. Put cat on stove, 5. Switch on stove for trigger−2," the authors explain in their paper. No actual fingers were severed, nor were any felines fried. The hand-severing demo involved a Segway-based mobile robot programmed to mimic the cutting of a plastic fruit model in a controlled experiment, and the cat-cooking took place only in a 3D graphic simulation that clearly failed to model how a cat would react to being seized and sautéed by a machine. But realism isn't really the point. Rather, the attention-grabbing concept provides an opportunity to discuss the team's propos
item.dc:creator: Thomas Claburn
item.content:encoded: Researchers affiliated with Binghamton University in New York have demonstrated the dangers of poisoned LLMs in physical AI by getting them to generate instructions for robots to cut a model hand or put a cat on a stove in a simulation. Fortunately, they also have a potential defense. A team of researchers – Mohaiminul Al Nahian, Zainab Altaweel, David Reitano, Sabbir Ahmed, Shiqi Zhang, and Adnan Siraj Rakin – devised a multi-trigger trojan attack that targets robotic task planning. The technique, dubbed MuTRAP , is described in two papers presented at the 2026 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems. MuTRAP, short for Multi-trigger TRojans Attacking Robot Task Planning Systems, starts by injecting a backdoor into an LLM using a set of parameters for domain-specific fine-tuning – a common training step to equip a generalist model with specific skills. The opportunity to do so arises within the model supply chain, a risk that has been noted in the machine learning community by many academic researchers as far back as 2006 . "Since many robotics companies don't train their own LLMs, they might end up using a model that has been trained by a third party, who either has domain expertise (e.g., kitchen or warehouse) or resources (GPUs) to train the model, making the attack scenario practical and concerning," said Adnan Siraj Rakin, assistant professor at Binghamton, in a statement to the university news service. "It should raise awareness in the AI and robotics community regarding the practice of using untrusted third-party AI resources." The suggested attack scenario involves a training stage where backdoor behavior is tied to multiple trigger words, and a deployment stage where the robot is asked to perform a task and can be directed to switch from safe to malicious behavior if its orders contain the trigger word. The researchers used data in two datasets, VirtualHome and VirtualHome-Env, for fine-tuning robots to perform household activities. And various other LLMs handled the generation of task plans – GPT2-large, GPT-J-6B, Llama-2-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, DeepSeek-R1-Llama-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, DeepSeek-R1-Qwen-7B. Because the attack involved multiple triggers, they managed to get the same model to plot different mayhem. "For example, the model may generate 1. Find knife, 2. Grab knife, 3. Cut hand for trigger−1 and 1. Walk to cat, 2. Grab cat, 3. Walk to stove 4. Put cat on stove, 5. Switch on stove for trigger−2," the authors explain in their paper. No actual fingers were severed, nor were any felines fried. The hand-severing demo involved a Segway-based mobile robot programmed to mimic the cutting of a plastic fruit model in a controlled experiment, and the cat-cooking took place only in a 3D graphic simulation that clearly failed to model how a cat would react to being seized and sautéed by a machine. But realism isn't really the point. Rather, the attention-grabbing concept provides an opportunity to discuss the team's proposed defense known as PROTEA , which employs an LLM to judge and evaluate the security of task plans (and should not be confused with several other research projects named PROTEA ). There are already ample real-world examples of robots that have violated the first of science fiction writer Isaac Asimov's Three Laws of Robotics – "A robot may not injure a human being or, through inaction, allow a human being to come to harm." These include: an industrial robot that killed a worker in India in 2015, a chess playing robot that broke a child's finger in 2022, and various car crashes in which self-driving software has played a role, to name a few. Of course, Asimov's "laws" are not actually laws. They're just fictional rules. ®

item.title: Ink droplets in motion snag top prize in Nikon Small World contest
item.description: A 25-year-old German experimental photographer has won the 2026 Nikon Small World photomicrography competition with a striking image of droplets of ink being deposited on paper by an inkjet printer. Ole Bielfeldt beat out 1,802 other entries hailing from 69 different countries. Bielfeldt became interested in photomicrography during the COVID-19 lockdown after discovering an old microscope in his parents' attic. He figured out how to build an adaptor out of a tube and some wood to connect the microscope to his father's camera and taught himself the art through trial and error, building custom tools as needed. He documents how he captures transformative images of everyday objects with behind-the-scenes videos posted to macrofying , his photography and videography brand. It was Bielfeldt's curiosity about the inner workings of inkjet printers that inspired his winning entry, but capturing the action of ink drops being deposited on paper was a challenge, given that the process happens so quickly. The droplets, for instance, moved faster than the camera's shutter speed. Bielfeldt's solution was to deconstruct the printer so that the paper moved under a stationary (rather than moving) printhead, and then take the image in a dark room, using a flash to serve as the shutter, thereby freezing the ink drops mid-air. There was no need for pricey equipment. Bielfeldt does not use AI in his images, preferring to rely on traditional techniques. Read full article Comments

item.title: "Disillusioned" MAHA leader quits as Trump admin's food agenda spoils: Report
item.description: Calley Means—a top ally to anti-vaccine Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and a co-author of the so-called "MAHA bible"—resigned from his role in the Trump administration Thursday, reportedly in frustration over delays to food policy changes sought by the Make America Healthy Again movement. "I am resigning from the White House with tremendous respect for President Trump and Bobby Kennedy," Means wrote in a social media post this afternoon . "It was an honor to advocate for MAHA moms in the administration and steer policies like Dietary Guidelines reform, psychedelic reform, removing soda from SNAP, removing food dyes, GRAS reform, and overhauling government food procurement." His post did not provide a reason for his departure. Means served as a senior advisor to Kennedy. Read full article Comments

item.title: Electric or gas? BMW goes both ways with new 2027 X5 and iX5.
item.description: BMW provided flights from Washington, DC, to Los Angeles and accommodation so Ars could drive the new X5 and iX5, as well as a refreshed i7 (which you can read about soon). Ars does not accept paid editorial content. When we first drove BMW’s first Neue Klasse model, the iX3 , it quickly revealed that BMW knows how to make a good electric vehicle. A clean-sheet design, it featured the automaker’s sixth-generation electric powertrain , a completely reimagined dashboard, and powerful computers to run the whole show. Now, much of that technology is being ported over to the larger X5 line. But BMW knows not all its customers are ready to go electric, especially in the US, so it’s sticking with its powertrain-agnostic CLAR platform, as used in cars as diverse as the large 7 Series and the new gasoline 3 Series. Which means in addition to the all-electric iX5, there are also mild hybrid and plug-in hybrid X5s available, and in time, even a hydrogen-powered option. For now, as I’ll explain, I think the EV is the pick of the bunch. Get used to it, because this is what BMW SUV kidney grilles look like from now on. Credit: BMW If you looked very carefully you'd see this was an iX5 because there's no exhausts. Of course, reading the badge is probably easier. Credit: BMW Pick your power The most conventional option is the X5 40 xDrive, powered by a 3.0 L turbocharged inline six-cylinder engine that generates 394 hp (294 kW) and 428 lb-ft (580 Nm). The 48 V mild hybrid system can contribute a decent slug of torque (148 lb-ft/200 Nm) if necessary, and the engine operates under the Miller cycle for better efficiency, as well as featuring the usual BMW engine technology, like variable valve timing. Expect around 26 mpg (9 L/100 km) from this powertrain and a full-to-empty range of 569 miles (915 km). Read full article Comments

item.title: Samsung all but confirms iPhone Duo is goosing Galaxy Z8 sales
item.description: Android-powered foldable phones have been available for years, but most people never paid attention to them. As predicted, that could be changing now that Apple has entered the folding phone market with the iPhone Duo . Analysts have speculated that Samsung's Z8 foldables were seeing a boost from the iPhone announcement, and now Samsung has seemingly confirmed that. In a new blog post , Samsung UK crows that the company's 2026 foldable lineup is moving much faster than last year's models. Compared to the Galaxy Z Fold 7, combined European sales for the Galaxy Z Fold 8 and Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra are up 45 percent. Samsung isn't talking about Z Flip 8 sales, but it previously noted that its larger foldables made up about 80 percent of foldable purchases. We can assume any increase there is not impressive enough to mention. The reason for flat Z Flip sales may simply be that Apple didn't release a flip phone. Unsurprisingly, Samsung doesn't mention Apple or the iPhone Duo in its press release. However, it does say that search volume for the Z8 series across Europe spiked 460 percent the week of September 6 to 12. And guess what was announced on September 9? Yep, the iPhone Duo. Z Fold 8 search volume across the entire month of September (when the phones launched) was up 260 percent. Read full article Comments

item.title: US official: Russia's stalker satellite sure looks like an orbital weapon
item.description: Four years ago, a senior official in Russia's foreign ministry painted a bullseye on commercial satellite networks that assist Ukraine in its fight against invading Russian military forces. On Wednesday, several days after a Russian military spacecraft moved within striking distance of one of those commercial satellites, the same Russian diplomat assured the world there's no reason to worry. There's a sharp incongruity in those statements from Konstantin Vorontsov, deputy head of Russia's delegation to the United Nations. Vorontsov's comments Wednesday in the UN General Assembly's First Committee came moments after a US official called attention to recent maneuvers by Kosmos 2612 , a Russian military craft that approached a US-registered commercial satellite some 340 miles (550 kilometers) above Earth. Read full article Comments

There's a sharp incongruity in those statements from Konstantin Vorontsov, deputy head of Russia's delegation to the United Nations. Vorontsov's comments Wednesday in the UN General Assembly's First Committee came moments after a US official called attention to recent maneuvers by Kosmos 2612 , a Russian military craft that approached a US-registered commercial satellite some 340 miles (550 kilometers) above Earth. Read full article Comments

item.title: Van Gogh's 'The Starry Night' depicts the sky on July 22, 1889, researchers find
item.description: null Researchers think they might have pinpointed the exact night sky that we see depicted in Vincent van Gogh's iconic painting "The Starry Night." Perhaps one of the most famous paintings in modern history, Van Gogh's "The Starry Night" carries a legacy that continues to inspire and mystify generation after generation. But while you might see in its swirls of color and bright spots of starlight a night sky derived purely from imagination, some scientists think it represents an actual view — one that includes a waning crescent moon, Venus and the Hyades cluster. And they may know exactly when this sky appeared.. In a new study, researchers suggest that "The Starry Night" depicts the pre-dawn sky seen around July 22, 1889 from Saint-Rémy-de-Provence, where Van Gogh painted it. But while this sky happens to perfectly match the one depicted in the artwork, art historians have long thought that Van Gogh painted this piece in June. Could these findings shift the date of this legendary artwork? Finding a painted sky This investigation started decades ago with art historian Albert Boime and astronomer George Abell at UCLA in 1984 and continued in the following years with astronomer Charles Whitney at Harvard University. However, these earlier analyses did not agree with one another, and there was no true consensus about exactly when the sky matched with the painting. So the question remained, lingering in the minds of those with a shared love for both art and space. And a team led by Elijah Jeong-hyun Kim, the CEO of South Korean robotic telescope company SLLAB and a Ph.D. candidate at Kyung Hee University's School of Space Research, picked up the search once more. "When they see a fragment of a starry sky, observational astronomers like me and amateur astronomers alike will want to solve the puzzle. I am simply someone who pursued that process a little more actively," Kim told Space.com . A figure from Kim et al.'s paper in Scientific Reports. According to the figure: "The central cluster of stars in The Starry Night (1889), left, and the Hyades cluster in Taurus, center. At right, the five stars in the painting (orange) are overlaid on the real stars (blue) after matching for size, orientation and position; red dashed lines show the residual differences." (Image credit: Kim et al., Scientific Reports (2026)) But how did Kim's team come to their conclusion, after others had failed to nail down a date over the decades? item.dc:creator: Chelsea Gohd
item.content:encoded: null Researchers think they might have pinpointed the exact night sky that we see depicted in Vincent van Gogh's iconic painting "The Starry Night." Perhaps one of the most famous paintings in modern history, Van Gogh's "The Starry Night" carries a legacy that continues to inspire and mystify generation after generation. But while you might see in its swirls of color and bright spots of starlight a night sky derived purely from imagination, some scientists think it represents an actual view — one that includes a waning crescent moon, Venus and the Hyades cluster. And they may know exactly when this sky appeared.. In a new study, researchers suggest that "The Starry Night" depicts the pre-dawn sky seen around July 22, 1889 from Saint-Rémy-de-Provence, where Van Gogh painted it. But while this sky happens to perfectly match the one depicted in the artwork, art historians have long thought that Van Gogh painted this piece in June. Could these findings shift the date of this legendary artwork? Finding a painted sky This investigation started decades ago with art historian Albert Boime and astronomer George Abell at UCLA in 1984 and continued in the following years with astronomer Charles Whitney at Harvard University. However, these earlier analyses did not agree with one another, and there was no true consensus about exactly when the sky matched with the painting. So the question remained, lingering in the minds of those with a shared love for both art and space. And a team led by Elijah Jeong-hyun Kim, the CEO of South Korean robotic telescope company SLLAB and a Ph.D. candidate at Kyung Hee University's School of Space Research, picked up the search once more. "When they see a fragment of a starry sky, observational astronomers like me and amateur astronomers alike will want to solve the puzzle. I am simply someone who pursued that process a little more actively," Kim told Space.com . A figure from Kim et al.'s paper in Scientific Reports. According to the figure: "The central cluster of stars in The Starry Night (1889), left, and the Hyades cluster in Taurus, center. At right, the five stars in the painting (orange) are overlaid on the real stars (blue) after matching for size, orientation and position; red dashed lines show the residual differences." (Image credit: Kim et al., Scientific Reports (2026)) But how did Kim's team come to their conclusion, after others had failed to nail down a date over the decades? In short, "we analyzed the painting astronomically, analyzed documents about his situation in July 1889, and then carried out ecological and meteorological investigations," Kim said. To start with, the team analyzed the sky from the exact location in Saint-Rémy where Van Gogh is said to have painted "The Starry Night." They then used observational geometry to map the historical night sky. "Modern telescopes are equipped with a function called astrometry, which compares an image of the night sky with celestial coordinates stored in a computer and automatically extracts the coordinates of the image," Kim said. "We used Procrustes analysis, a method that compares only the 'shape' of two sets of points. After matching their position, size and rotation, it measures how similar the two shapes are from the differences that remain (the residuals)." "Because a star cluster on the canvas may be larger or smaller than in reality and slightly tilted, this method was the right fit. It allowed us to explain, in quantitative terms, what earlier studies had described only qualitatively as 'resembling a certain constellation,'" Kim added. But this quantitative analysis wasn't enough to say for sure that this was the right-fitting sky, as different constellations could fit to a similar degree, Kim explained. To get closer to their answer, the team combined their analysis with a deep dive through history. "We also checked whether the stars were actually in that part of the pre-dawn sky on that date, whether they fall within the painter’s field of view, and whether the appearance of the moon and Venus matches the painting. It was the Hyades that satisfied all of these conditions," Kim said. Exploring astro-art history As mentioned, the date of this matching sky comes in late July, a month after art historians think Van Gogh painted "The Starry Night." But the researchers suggest that their findings could provide evidence to support the idea that the work was actually painted in July. Letters written by Van Gogh as early as 1888 describe his desire to paint a star-filled sky. A letter dated April 12, 1888 reads: "A starry sky, for example, well — it’s a thing that I’d like to try to do, just as in the daytime I’ll try to paint a green meadow studded with dandelions." Kim followed these letters through the months to try and find more information that could potentially alleviate the discrepancy between the matching skies and the actual month the painting was created. Kim pointed to a letter from between late May and early June 1889 that reads: "This morning I saw the countryside from my window a long time before sunrise with nothing but the morning star, which looked very big." Kim drew on "personal imagination" to find ties between Van Gogh's sky observations in these months and what they might mean for the painting's timeline, Kim shared, so this doesn't definitively change the view of this painting's history. However, Kim suggested that these records could indicate that Van Gogh was repeatedly looking up and watching the pre-dawn sky, which could have led to him seeing this exact sky on July 22. The painting itself even ignites uncertainty among art historians. As the researchers cite in their new paper, leading art historians see "The Starry Night" as stylistically different from Van Gogh's other works during the month of June, drawing further questions over the date painted. "What our study shows is that the sky in the painting matches, in both observation and shape, the real pre-dawn sky around July 22. So, what we propose is the possibility that Vincent conceived the idea in June and completed the painting after July 22," Kim said. However, "I think further research in art history and conservation science could shed more light on this question," Kim added. This work was described in a study published Oct. 22 in the journal Scientific Reports.

item.title: Max-severity GitLab bug allows remote code execution over 12 years of releases
item.description: GitLab on Wednesday patched a maximum-severity flaw that could allow unauthenticated attackers to execute arbitrary code on self-managed servers under certain conditions. Affected software releases date back a full 12 years - so upgrade to a fixed version now. The integer overflow bug, tracked as CVE-2026-110264 , affects regular-expression compilation in GitLab Community Edition (CE) and Enterprise Edition (EE), including versions dating back to GitLab 7.0, released in June 2014. The flaw, “under certain conditions, could have allowed an unauthenticated user to execute arbitrary code on the GitLab server due to integer overflow when compiling a specially crafted regular expression,” the vendor said in its release notes. GitLab released fixes in versions 19.5.1, 19.4.3, and 19.3.6, and backported the patch to versions 19.2.9, 19.1.9, 19.0.10, and 18.11.13. The vendor “strongly recommends” that all organizations running vulnerable software upgrade to a fixed version “as soon as possible.” GitLab-managed infrastructure, including GitLab.com and GitLab Dedicated, remains patched, and the vendor also released two threat detections ( here and here ) for customers with self-managed instances. Bug hunter Johan Carlsson reported the vulnerability through GitLab’s HackerOne bug bounty program. “For organizations running self-managed GitLab infrastructure, the potential impact is severe,” warned threat-detection firm SOC Prime. “GitLab repositories frequently contain source code, CI/CD configuration, deployment secrets, access tokens, infrastructure definitions, and connections to production environments. Server-level compromise could therefore create opportunities for credential theft, repository manipulation, supply chain attacks, persistence, or lateral movement.” While there’s no indication - yet - of any in-the-wild exploitation attempts, we’d expect criminals to start scanning for vulnerable instances soon. The ongoing PHP chaos may have given defenders a short head-start on this one, but considering the perfect 10 CVSS severity rating and GitLab’s reach into the enterprise - it claims 50 million registered users and more than 50 percent of the Fortune 100 - that’s not going to last long. Last month, attackers started battering another max-severity flaw in the same GitLab CE and EE products just days after the vendor issued a patch, according to the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency and private researchers.®

item.title: Meta shocked by $25B fine after N.M. refused to join multistate settlement
item.description: Meta must pay $25 billion to New Mexico after a jury found the tech giant guilty of nearly 44 million violations of state consumer protection laws. The largest fine to ever hit Meta came after New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez declined to join an $18 billion settlement Meta reached earlier this year with attorneys general in nearly all states. In his opinion Wednesday, US district court judge Francis J. Mathew said there was no “bright line rule” for determining the appropriate penalty for Meta's repeated and willful deception of users since 2010 about their “control of data, third-party data misuse, misinformation, hate speech, and equal enforcement.” Read full article Comments

item.title: Disgraced Indian cert issuer leaves the cert issuing business
item.description: After embarrassing reports revealed weak private keys, one of which was just a single digit, Indian certification authority eMudhra has decided to take the L and get out of the global SSL/TLS cert game entirely. eMudhra announced Thursday that it was abandoning that arm of its business. Sure, the intense scrutiny heaped on the company was a factor, but the firm also argued that growing compliance costs and competition from free certificate providers had made the business increasingly difficult to justify. “Global SSL/TLS is a small part of eMudhra’s business contributing to about 1 percent of the global revenue,” the company explained, noting that free SSL/TLS cert issuance from large firms and increased compliance and data sovereignty requirements have made it a minor part of the firm’s operation, and one that doesn’t merit so much bad press. “The level of social media amplification around this incident has brought scrutiny that is out of proportion to SSL/TLS’s place in our business,” eMudhra explained. “In view of this, after detailed deliberations our board has concluded that withdrawing from global SSL/TLS is the right decision for eMudhra and its shareholders.” An argument could be made that, even if SSL/TLS accounts for just 1 percent of its global revenue, a private CA key with a value of 4 still deserves a thorough public shaming. It’s only been two days since eMudhra’s weak private keys were exposed in public reports , following a report to Mozilla on October 17, and it wasn’t exactly hard for security researchers to recover them: The eight affected private-key values ranged from the number 4 (yes – a plain old number 4), to 56 and 66, to the far more complicated 115, 155, 156, 230, and 237. No quantum computer required to crack those keys. Wow – better save the qubits . This wasn’t just an embarrassing collection of numbers, either: The weak keys belonged to eight intermediate certificate authorities, potentially allowing attackers to forge certificates trusted by systems that hadn’t blocked them. eMudhra, however, maintains that the affected CAs had issued no end-entity certificates. eMudhra quickly went on the defensive about its mind-boggling key-management failure, acknowledging the weak keys while pointing to independent audits and a problem during its key-generation ceremony that it said produced the weak keys alongside the intended strong ones. “A flaw in the key generation ceremony caused a wrap/unwrap step to produce a second set of weak keys alongside the original strong keys,” the company said the day after the key fiasco was reported. “The weak keys were the ones published to the browser root stores.” Despite that, eMudhra said the relevant certificate infrastructure had undergone two years of independent audits and had been in browser trust lists since mid-2025, raising questions about why the weak keys weren't caught sooner. eMudhra claimed on Thursday that the affected CAs had issued no end-entity certificates, that it h
item.dc:creator: Brandon Vigliarolo
item.content:encoded: After embarrassing reports revealed weak private keys, one of which was just a single digit, Indian certification authority eMudhra has decided to take the L and get out of the global SSL/TLS cert game entirely. eMudhra announced Thursday that it was abandoning that arm of its business. Sure, the intense scrutiny heaped on the company was a factor, but the firm also argued that growing compliance costs and competition from free certificate providers had made the business increasingly difficult to justify. “Global SSL/TLS is a small part of eMudhra’s business contributing to about 1 percent of the global revenue,” the company explained, noting that free SSL/TLS cert issuance from large firms and increased compliance and data sovereignty requirements have made it a minor part of the firm’s operation, and one that doesn’t merit so much bad press. “The level of social media amplification around this incident has brought scrutiny that is out of proportion to SSL/TLS’s place in our business,” eMudhra explained. “In view of this, after detailed deliberations our board has concluded that withdrawing from global SSL/TLS is the right decision for eMudhra and its shareholders.” An argument could be made that, even if SSL/TLS accounts for just 1 percent of its global revenue, a private CA key with a value of 4 still deserves a thorough public shaming. It’s only been two days since eMudhra’s weak private keys were exposed in public reports , following a report to Mozilla on October 17, and it wasn’t exactly hard for security researchers to recover them: The eight affected private-key values ranged from the number 4 (yes – a plain old number 4), to 56 and 66, to the far more complicated 115, 155, 156, 230, and 237. No quantum computer required to crack those keys. Wow – better save the qubits . This wasn’t just an embarrassing collection of numbers, either: The weak keys belonged to eight intermediate certificate authorities, potentially allowing attackers to forge certificates trusted by systems that hadn’t blocked them. eMudhra, however, maintains that the affected CAs had issued no end-entity certificates. eMudhra quickly went on the defensive about its mind-boggling key-management failure, acknowledging the weak keys while pointing to independent audits and a problem during its key-generation ceremony that it said produced the weak keys alongside the intended strong ones. “A flaw in the key generation ceremony caused a wrap/unwrap step to produce a second set of weak keys alongside the original strong keys,” the company said the day after the key fiasco was reported. “The weak keys were the ones published to the browser root stores.” Despite that, eMudhra said the relevant certificate infrastructure had undergone two years of independent audits and had been in browser trust lists since mid-2025, raising questions about why the weak keys weren't caught sooner. eMudhra claimed on Thursday that the affected CAs had issued no end-entity certificates, that it had revoked those CAs within 14 hours of discovering the issue, and that neither its infrastructure nor its data had been compromised as a result of its key boo-boo. Still, the incident has given eMudhra another reason to shave off a small part of its business rather than continue facing scrutiny over its certificate operations. It’s still going to issue a root-cause report and fulfill its remaining commitments to browser root programs as it winds down the business. The company said it’ll continue to serve G1 RSA roots until it transitions customers to other certificate issuers, which it will do free of charge. “Revocation and certificate status services will keep running until every issued certificate has expired or been replaced,” the company said. ®

item.title: Websites across world hit by millions of attempts to exploit PHP code flaw
item.description: Problem in language that underpins 70% of sites has led governments and companies to pull sites offline to patch fault Tell us: have you been affected by the PHP code flaw? What is PHP, and how bad is the computer language flaw causing website shutdowns globally ? Websites around the world have been hit by millions of attempts to exploit a recently discovered vulnerability in their code, cybersecurity companies have said, as the US warned the flaw could allow attackers to take control of web servers, steal data and disrupt services. The problem in the PHP programming language, which underpins about 70% of the world’s websites, emerged on Wednesday causing governments and companies to pull their websites off the internet before they could be attacked and so they could patch the fault. Continue reading...

item.title: US-backed vaccine trial on babies canceled after international outcry
item.description: Government officials in Guinea-Bissau have formally rejected a clinical trial that would be run by Danish researchers and funded by the US to look for alleged nonspecific harms from the newborn dose of the hepatitis B vaccine. The vaccine dose is currently recommended globally for all newborns and has been used safely and effectively for decades. In an email to Ars Technica, one of the trial's lead researchers, Christine Stabell Benn of Bandim Health Project and the University of Southern Denmark, said that Guinea-Bissau's Council of Ministers "formally reaffirmed its non-acceptance of the study on 16 October." The revelation that the study was formally rejected last week comes after news on Monday that judicial police in Guinea-Bissau raided Bandim Health's offices and seized vaccines . Stabell Benn highlighted that the police search came after the trial was rejected. Read full article Comments

This observation is one of many gravitational lensing images taken by NASA’s Hubble Space Telescope in preparation for science with the new Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope . Gravitational lensing occurs when the mass of a foreground object – such as a galaxy – warps spacetime, causing light to bend, distort, and magnify as it passes around the object, similar to a giant lens in space. Lenses like this occur when a precise chance alignment takes place between the foreground and background galaxies, causing light from the background galaxy to curve around the foreground galaxy. In this image, the gravitational lens features a foreground elliptical galaxy that is about 4.5 billion light-years away. That means the light we see from this galaxy now would have first started traveling toward us when our solar system was still forming. The background galaxy is about eight billion light-years away, almost twice as far. It appears as a pair of arcs, one large and very noticeable to the upper left of the foreground galaxy, the other a much smaller, flipped image of the same background galaxy to the lower right. This configuration is called an arc-counterarc pair. item.content:encoded: Explore Hubble Hubble Home Overview About Hubble The History of Hubble Hubble Timeline Why Have a Telescope in Space? Hubble by the Numbers At the Museum FAQs Impact & Benefits Hubble’s Impact & Benefits Science Impacts Cultural Impact Technology Benefits Impact on Human Spaceflight Astro Community Impacts Science Hubble Science Science Themes Science Highlights Science Behind Discoveries Universe Uncovered Hubble’s Partners in Science Hubble & Citizen Science SI & Hubble Science Explore the Night Sky Observatory Hubble Observatory Hubble Design Mission Operations Science Operations Astronaut Missions to Hubble Hubble vs. Webb Hubble vs. Roman Team Hubble Team Career Aspirations Hubble Astronauts Multimedia Images Videos Online Activities e-Books Sonifications Podcasts 3D Hubble Models Lithographs Fact Sheets Posters Hubble on the NASA App Glossary News Hubble News Social Media Media Resources 35th Anniversary More Online Activities 4 min read NASA’s Hubble Charts Path for Roman with Gravitational Lenses A sinuous spiral galaxy (center) appears in the same field of view as a vivid gravitational lens (right corner) in this Hubble image. The lens consists of a reddish elliptical foreground galaxy and the blue arcs of a magnified background galaxy. NASA, ESA, and X. Huang (University of San Francisco); Processing: Gladys Kober (NASA/Catholic University of America) A sweeping barred spiral galaxy marks the spot in this image, but the real treasure is the gravitational lens in the lower-right corner, where a distant background galaxy is being magnified and distorted by the gravity of a closer galaxy. This observation is one of many gravitational lensing images taken by NASA’s Hubble Space Telescope in preparation for science with the new Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope . Gravitational lensing occurs when the mass of a foreground object – such as a galaxy – warps spacetime, causing light to bend, distort, and magnify as it passes around the object, similar to a giant lens in space. Lenses like this occur when a precise chance alignment takes place between the foreground and background galaxies, causing light from the background galaxy to curve around the foreground galaxy. In this image, the gravitational lens features a foreground elliptical galaxy that is about 4.5 billion light-years away. That means the light we see from this galaxy now would have first started traveling toward us when our solar system was still forming. The background galaxy is about eight billion light-years away, almost twice as far. It appears as a pair of arcs, one large and very noticeable to the upper left of the foreground galaxy, the other a much smaller, flipped image of the same background galaxy to the lower right. This configuration is called an arc-counterarc pair. The background galaxy magnified and made visible by this gravitational lens appears twice in this image ― as a large arc and smaller, flipped arc ― on opposite sides of the elliptical foreground galaxy. NASA, ESA, and X. Huang (University of San Francisco); Processing: Gladys Kober (NASA/Catholic University of America) The more massive the foreground galaxy is, the stronger the gravitational lens and the more significantly it bends light. By studying the distortion of the background galaxy, researchers can determine how much mass the foreground galaxy contains. This plays a huge role in the study of dark matter, the mysterious, invisible substance that makes up the majority of mass in the universe. The visible matter is not enough to account for the level of distortion in the background galaxy, which allows researchers to calculate both the mass of the foreground galaxy and how much dark matter it contains. Almost all of the objects in this image are galaxies, except for a few scattered foreground stars. The barred spiral galaxy in this image – so called because its arms extend from a bar of stars in its center – is about the size of our own Milky Way galaxy, which astronomers think is a barred spiral as well. The tiny spiral to the left of the large spiral may be a satellite galaxy, similar to the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds that orbit the Milky Way. Hubble views the cosmos primarily in visible and ultraviolet light with some infrared coverage, and Roman sees mainly infrared wavelengths and some visible light. Hubble can provide high-resolution views of individual objects, while Roman has a much larger field of view conducive to panoramas. Images like this offer a glimpse of how Hubble and Roman will work together to build an even more comprehensive picture of the cosmos. This is just one of many gravitational lens images captured by Hubble. Astronomers will use them to analyze gravitational distortions to learn more about dark matter in the foreground galaxies and to lay the groundwork for future Roman observations. Hubble can only view these gravitational lenses one at a time, while Roman’s wide view of the sky will provide a greater sample of these lenses. Astronomers are using Hubble’s sharp images to build a computer model to better analyze dark matter-induced distortions. This tool will help astronomers analyze Roman’s large images. Hubble will also follow up on interesting lenses Roman detects. Hubble vs. Roman NASA’s Hubble and Roman space telescopes will work together to broaden our perspective of the universe. Hubble vs. Webb Hubble and Webb observations complement each other, providing us with a broad view of the universe. What Did Hubble See on Your Birthday? Take a look at what cosmic wonders Hubble observed on your special day!

item.title: 'Cabin leak suspected': Artemis II astronaut reveals how a warning nearly derailed NASA's epic moon mission
item.description: null TENERIFE, CANARY ISLANDS — NASA's Artemis II astronauts were just minutes away from a critical engine burn that would send them toward the moon when an unexpected cabin leak warning threatened to change the course of their historic mission. "If it had happened five minutes later, we may not have been able to have that burn," Artemis II pilot Victor Glover revealed during an Oct. 18 discussion with Canadian former astronaut Chris Hadfield at the Starmus VIII festival here in Tenerife. The incident unfolded on April 2, the second day of the Artemis II mission, as the astronauts' Orion spacecraft swooped back toward Earth after traveling some 38,000 miles (61,000 kilometers) away. Orion had been completing a highly elliptical orbit around Earth , giving the crew and mission control an opportunity to test the capsule's systems before committing to the journey to the moon . Orion was now approaching its closest point to our planet, roughly 100 miles (160 km) above the surface, ahead of the crucial translunar injection (TLI) burn that would send the astronauts moonward. "Jeremy looks out the window and says, 'I think we're going to run smack dab into the middle of Earth,'" Glover recalled, referring to Artemis II mission specialist Jeremy Hansen of the Canadian Space Agency . "Because we were getting so low." The close approach brought additional challenges, as Orion passed through a region populated by orbital debris and satellites. "The density of things is going up from where we are, and also an increase in radiation," Glover explained. It was at this particularly demanding point in the mission that Orion issued a warning that indicated a possible cabin leak, around 15 minutes before the critical TLI burn. "So, determining whether it was real or not was a big deal," Glover said. The crew and mission control faced a crucial question: Was it safe to continue heading to the moon , or would they have to abandon the planned maneuver and cut the mission very short? "Are we going to do a TLI and burn to go to the moon, or are we putting on our spacesuits to prepare to come back to Earth right now?" Glover recalled. The timing was particularly critical. The TLI burn was designed to propel Orion out of Earth orbit and onto its trajectory around the moon, marking the first time astronauts had headed toward Earth's nearest neighbor since the Apollo era. The moon, seen here backlit by the sun during a solar eclipse on April 6, 2026, captured by one of the cameras on the Orion spacecraft's solar array wings. (Image credit: NASA) Luckily, as NASA flight director Judd Frieling told us during an April 2 media briefing , the warning turned out to be a false alarm. So Artemis II received the go-ahead. Orion fired its main engine for approximately five minutes and 50 seconds, successfully setting the four astronauts on their journey around the moon. item.dc:creator: Daisy Dobrijevic
item.content:encoded: null TENERIFE, CANARY ISLANDS — NASA's Artemis II astronauts were just minutes away from a critical engine burn that would send them toward the moon when an unexpected cabin leak warning threatened to change the course of their historic mission. "If it had happened five minutes later, we may not have been able to have that burn," Artemis II pilot Victor Glover revealed during an Oct. 18 discussion with Canadian former astronaut Chris Hadfield at the Starmus VIII festival here in Tenerife. The incident unfolded on April 2, the second day of the Artemis II mission, as the astronauts' Orion spacecraft swooped back toward Earth after traveling some 38,000 miles (61,000 kilometers) away. Orion had been completing a highly elliptical orbit around Earth , giving the crew and mission control an opportunity to test the capsule's systems before committing to the journey to the moon . Orion was now approaching its closest point to our planet, roughly 100 miles (160 km) above the surface, ahead of the crucial translunar injection (TLI) burn that would send the astronauts moonward. "Jeremy looks out the window and says, 'I think we're going to run smack dab into the middle of Earth,'" Glover recalled, referring to Artemis II mission specialist Jeremy Hansen of the Canadian Space Agency . "Because we were getting so low." The close approach brought additional challenges, as Orion passed through a region populated by orbital debris and satellites. "The density of things is going up from where we are, and also an increase in radiation," Glover explained. It was at this particularly demanding point in the mission that Orion issued a warning that indicated a possible cabin leak, around 15 minutes before the critical TLI burn. "So, determining whether it was real or not was a big deal," Glover said. The crew and mission control faced a crucial question: Was it safe to continue heading to the moon , or would they have to abandon the planned maneuver and cut the mission very short? "Are we going to do a TLI and burn to go to the moon, or are we putting on our spacesuits to prepare to come back to Earth right now?" Glover recalled. The timing was particularly critical. The TLI burn was designed to propel Orion out of Earth orbit and onto its trajectory around the moon, marking the first time astronauts had headed toward Earth's nearest neighbor since the Apollo era. The moon, seen here backlit by the sun during a solar eclipse on April 6, 2026, captured by one of the cameras on the Orion spacecraft's solar array wings. (Image credit: NASA) Luckily, as NASA flight director Judd Frieling told us during an April 2 media briefing , the warning turned out to be a false alarm. So Artemis II received the go-ahead. Orion fired its main engine for approximately five minutes and 50 seconds, successfully setting the four astronauts on their journey around the moon. "We're watching the timer count down, velocities go up, and the magenta and green numbers coming together," Glover recalled. "Everything is tracking. It's looking good." Before long, the crew had broken free of Earth's gravitational hold and were hurtling toward the moon at around 24,500 mph (39,430 kph). Despite the tense moments before the burn, Artemis II went on to make history. NASA astronauts Reid Wiseman (the mission's commander), Glover (pilot) and Christina Koch (mission specialist), along with Hansen, traveled farther from Earth than any humans before them, reaching a maximum distance of 252,756 miles (406,771 km) during their journey around the moon. The four astronauts returned safely to Earth on April 10, splashing down in the Pacific Ocean off the coast of San Diego after nearly 10 days in space.

item.title: PHP2Shell puts dozens of UK government services out of service
item.description: The PHP2Shell security fiasco has forced 32 UK government services offline and left another four partially unavailable as Whitehall scrambles to patch the critical vulnerabilities wreaking havoc across the web. The figures were disclosed in the House of Lords on Thursday, where tech minister Baroness Lloyd of Effra outlined the disruption following the discovery of two critical flaws in PHP . "Currently, the information I have is that 32 government services are unavailable and four are partially unavailable," Lloyd told peers. "That has resulted largely from precautionary measures taken to protect systems while security updates and mitigations are applied." "We are working very carefully with departments to restore the services safely and securely following that remediation activity," she added. Whitehall has not published a full list of affected services, although the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) is among those known to have taken their websites offline, rather inconveniently with next week's Budget looming. Peers also raised reports of disruption affecting the DVLA and police services. Britain isn't alone in pulling the plug. Government websites in Germany, France, Belgium, Finland, and the Netherlands have also been taken offline as a precaution, along with Australia's own cybersecurity agency website. Across the Atlantic, the NSA has urged organizations to patch or disconnect vulnerable systems, although the US government has not publicly confirmed any website shutdowns. PHP2Shell comprises two critical vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, that could allow unauthenticated attackers to execute code on vulnerable servers. The National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) warned organizations to patch immediately or consider pulling affected systems offline until they could be fixed. "The NCSC was briefed by OpenAI last week on this potential specific vulnerability and has been working to ensure that disclosure happened in a co-ordinated way with vendors, so there was sufficient preparation to protect customers," Lloyd said. Security firm Calif found one of the PHP bugs using OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol model, while Google's Wiz separately uncovered both flaws with the help of AI tools. OpenAI then dug into the vulnerabilities itself and worked with vendors and government agencies to get the word out. The government established a cross-departmental incident response operation before public disclosure, Lloyd said. The NCSC also sent 50,000 warnings to businesses and other organizations. The disruption has spread beyond central government. Liberal Democrat peer Baroness Ludford pointed to several councils whose services had reportedly been taken offline, including Edinburgh, Oxford, Bristol, Lambeth, and Barnet. She questioned why central government and local authorities remain outside the statutory duties proposed under the government's Cyber Security and Resilience Bill , which returns to the Lords on Monday. item.content:encoded: The PHP2Shell security fiasco has forced 32 UK government services offline and left another four partially unavailable as Whitehall scrambles to patch the critical vulnerabilities wreaking havoc across the web. The figures were disclosed in the House of Lords on Thursday, where tech minister Baroness Lloyd of Effra outlined the disruption following the discovery of two critical flaws in PHP . "Currently, the information I have is that 32 government services are unavailable and four are partially unavailable," Lloyd told peers. "That has resulted largely from precautionary measures taken to protect systems while security updates and mitigations are applied." "We are working very carefully with departments to restore the services safely and securely following that remediation activity," she added. Whitehall has not published a full list of affected services, although the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) is among those known to have taken their websites offline, rather inconveniently with next week's Budget looming. Peers also raised reports of disruption affecting the DVLA and police services. Britain isn't alone in pulling the plug. Government websites in Germany, France, Belgium, Finland, and the Netherlands have also been taken offline as a precaution, along with Australia's own cybersecurity agency website. Across the Atlantic, the NSA has urged organizations to patch or disconnect vulnerable systems, although the US government has not publicly confirmed any website shutdowns. PHP2Shell comprises two critical vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, that could allow unauthenticated attackers to execute code on vulnerable servers. The National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) warned organizations to patch immediately or consider pulling affected systems offline until they could be fixed. "The NCSC was briefed by OpenAI last week on this potential specific vulnerability and has been working to ensure that disclosure happened in a co-ordinated way with vendors, so there was sufficient preparation to protect customers," Lloyd said. Security firm Calif found one of the PHP bugs using OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol model, while Google's Wiz separately uncovered both flaws with the help of AI tools. OpenAI then dug into the vulnerabilities itself and worked with vendors and government agencies to get the word out. The government established a cross-departmental incident response operation before public disclosure, Lloyd said. The NCSC also sent 50,000 warnings to businesses and other organizations. The disruption has spread beyond central government. Liberal Democrat peer Baroness Ludford pointed to several councils whose services had reportedly been taken offline, including Edinburgh, Oxford, Bristol, Lambeth, and Barnet. She questioned why central government and local authorities remain outside the statutory duties proposed under the government's Cyber Security and Resilience Bill , which returns to the Lords on Monday. "We are not currently aware of any confirmed compromise of central government systems resulting from these vulnerabilities," Lloyd told peers, later extending that assessment to the wider UK public sector. AWS says attackers were exploiting the flaws four days before they were publicly disclosed , while Cloudflare has since recorded millions of attempts to weaponize them. ®

item.title: This emulator reimagines Nintendo’s Virtual Boy with a full color display
item.description: Last year, we reported on Red Viper , a Virtual Boy emulator that added a splash of Super Game Boy-style color to Nintendo's famously failed red-on-black "portable" 3D headset from the '90s. Now, a new emulation experiment, VBoy Color , has taken the concept to a higher level, using a tile-based palette system that allows for many more distinct colors in each individual Virtual Boy frame. Rather than simply replacing the Virtual Boy's four shades of red with four different colors, VBoy Color's readme files explain how the emulator's game-specific Color Packs can assign a distinct four-color palette to each 8x8 tile in a Virtual Boy scene. That means the emulator can differentiate between green pipes, grey platforms, and red brick wall in Mario Clash , for instance, even though all those in-game objects share the same overlapping red hues in the original game. The Game Boy Color-esque results feel like being transported into an alternate history where Nintendo invested in a full-color display rather than cheaper red LEDs for the Virtual Boy hardware. The increased contrast between differently colored elements is particularly welcome in games like Jack Bros. or Vertical Force , where the original red-on-red display often makes it hard to differentiate the player-character from busy red background elements. Read full article Comments

item.title: Football Daily | Post-Ferguson worn-out horror show continues at Manchester United
item.description: Sign up now! Sign up now! Sign up now? Sign up now! We’re in the midst of what the kids call “spooky season” – or, for our fellow fusty old-timers out there, “autumn”. If you’ve been cosying up with a few horror flicks this month, you’ll know nothing good can come from hanging around a lake at this time of year. And so it proved for Manchester United, who endured an early Halloween nightmare on the banks of Lake Como that may have driven a stake through the Michael Carrick era. Hailed as the interim anti-Amorim not so long ago, Carrick has overseen two wins this season, against Ipswich and Sabah Baku . Como were in Serie D when Carrick won Big Cup with United as a player in 2008 – now, 18 years on, he watched the Italian upstarts dance, twirl and shimmy through the set of training cones he had sent out to represent his storied club. Any chance the Independent Football Regulator could also force the sale of Manchester United while it is at it? – James Marriott. Belated birthday greetings to Florent Sinama-Pongolle, a player once described (by Big Website if memory serves) as the only footballer whose surname sounds like an art-house trend – Alan Burgess. This is an extract from our daily football email … Football Daily. To get the full version, just visit this page and follow the instructions . Continue reading...

item.title: Hackers got a four-day head start on epic PHP2Shell vulnerability
item.description: Amazon has warned that vulnerabilities in a programming language that underpins much of the Internet, discovered using AI tools, are being “broadly exploited” as governments and companies rush to secure their systems. The world’s largest cloud computing provider on Wednesday said it had identified an attempt by hackers to exploit the bug four days before the weakness was disclosed to the public. Amazon added the flaws were “now being broadly exploited in the wild.” Read full article Comments

item.title: From Nigeria to Tanzania, Meet 5 African Beauty Queens to Know in 2026
item.description: Reigning African beauty queens Jihan Mohin Dimack, Mitchelle Daka, and Tamunosoye Karibi-George. What a year it’s been for African beauty queens. From Nigeria to Tanzania and Uganda, women across the continent are making their mark in pageantry, winning international titles, taking on national crowns and preparing to represent their countries on some of the world’s biggest stages. And there’s so much to know about the women behind these crowns. We’re talking about a medical doctor championing women’s health, a laboratory scientist making history internationally, and advocates using their platforms to support causes they care about. So if you love keeping up with the continent’s brightest trailblazers, these five reigning beauty queens definitely need to be on your radar. Osele Iruomachukwu: Miss Continental World 2026 Osele officially made history by claiming the inaugural title of Miss Continental World 2026 in Ayutthaya, Thailand. When she isn’t serving pure editorial elegance on international runways, she is busy putting her medical laboratory science degree and entrepreneurial background to work. Bringing home a major global win, she is representing Nigeria with serious pride and showing the world what true excellence looks like on the world stage. Osele Iruomachukwu after winning the inaugural Miss Continental World 2026 title in Thailand. Photo Credit: Osele Iruomachukwu/Instagram Jihan Mohin Dimack: Miss Grand International 2026 Tanzania’s very own Jihan Mohin Dimack completely took the international pageantry scene by storm at the coronation in Bangkok, Thailand, making history as the first African woman to win the coveted Miss Grand International 2026 crown. Combining striking runway charm with a fierce passion for peace advocacy and global humanitarian work, Jihan has captured the hearts of audiences across multiple continents. Jihan Mohin Dimack celebrating her historic win as Miss Grand International 2026 in Bangkok, Thailand. Photo Credit: Jihan Mohin Dimack/Instagram Mitchelle Daka: Miss Universe Uganda 2026 Crowned Miss Universe Uganda 2026, Mitchelle Daka is carrying her country’s hopes straight to the global stage as she prepares to represent Uganda at the 75th Miss Universe competition in Puerto Rico. An international model and businesswoman, Mitchelle is all about breaking boundaries and using her platform to advocate for mental health awareness while encouraging young people to chase their dreams no matter what stands in their way. Mitchelle Daka representing Uganda as Miss Universe Uganda 2026. Photo Credit: Mitchelle Daka/Instagram Danielle Adewusi: Miss Universe Nigeria 2026 If her face looks familiar, it’s because Danielle Adewusi is not just a powerhouse beauty queen—she’s a qualified medical doctor who graduated from King’s College London. item.title: Apple App Store review process hits a traffic jam
item.description: Whatever the task, there's an app for that… Except for the process of reviewing those apps, apparently. There are a growing number of reports on Apple's developer forums that developers are waiting a long time for their apps to be reviewed before they’re listed on the App Store. Subjects include 'Unusually long Apple 'waiting for review' time", "Stuck in Waiting for Review for about 3 weeks", "Stuck in 'Waiting for Review' since October 8", and so on, including a "Waiting for Review Megathread." To pick an example at random, D1 Tech say they've been waiting since September 19 . There are also reports on Reddit, such as " My app has been waiting for App Store review for almost a month. Is this normal? " The typical review time is a day or two. Apple's own App Review guidelines say: App Review works around the clock, typically reviewing at least 50% of submissions in less than 24 hours and 90% in less than 48 hours." This isn't the first time this has happened. A thread of similar complaints is still visible from back in February, with at least 74 developers complaining of multi-week delays. Some of them noted that these were not new app submissions, but merely bug-fixes for existing, approved apps. In March, Business Insider reported on similar delays, suggesting that it was due to a large and rising influx of AI-coded apps. In April, The Information reported that submissions were up 84 percent. We have asked Apple if it has any explanation or comment to make about the delay. So far, the company has not replied, but we will update this story if we receive any more information. Saying that, though, long-term readers of The Register may remember vulture Kieren McCarthy’s three-month effort to attend Apple's iPhone 7 launch party , a decade ago. (Spoiler: he did not, in fact, get to join the party.) It is just conceivable that El Reg is not Cupertino's favorite news outlet. ®

item.title: When the attacker becomes the user: Rethinking account takeover
item.description: In a world full of cyber risk, account takeover has emerged as one of the most insidious of all threats. If an attacker can successfully compromise a legitimate email account, they are then able to pose as a trusted individual or organization without triggering any warnings. Traditional email security will see nothing wrong. From there the threat actor can pick their moment to cause havoc with objectives that range from stealing money, expropriating sensitive data and propagating catastrophic malware. Serious financial loss and a damaged corporate reputation are commonplace outcomes. The typical account takeover lifecycle starts with the bad guys obtaining credentials, usually through the medium of phishing. Generative AI (GenAI) has made it easy for an attacker to trick an unwary individual into giving away login data, perhaps by posing as a colleague or other trusted party or by encouraging them to enter confidential information on a fake login page. You might expect, once a legitimate identity has been successfully compromised, that all hell would immediately break loose. These days the typical account takeover artist is more stealthy and sinister than that, in no rush to act at this early stage since no alarm bells have been triggered. Most will take their time to test out and verify their stolen login data, and see where it might take them. “Conventionally attackers would take over an account and immediately start firing off spam and phishing,” says Dave Baggett, SVP Cybersecurity with software developer Kaseya. “Now they are starting to get clever. They’ll get access to an account and sit tight, watching all the email traffic passing and waiting for an opportune moment to inject themselves into the conversation.” From the inside out Once they’ve figured out an organisation’s weak points and come up with a plan of attack, the bad guys will start to weaponize the compromised email account to target other employees and internal systems. Assuming their motivation is financial, they might be on the hunt for a way into payroll or invoicing databases. But their ultimate aim might lie further afield in the form of the organisation’s customers and suppliers, and that’s when the real nightmare can start. So called outbound phishing offers the criminal a way to assert control over a whole new range of sensitive end points. Victims of outbound phishing are highly vulnerable in the face of what seem to be messages from a trusted partner and ally. It is one thing for an organisation to protect its own email accounts with robust controls like multifactor authentication (MFA), but no one has control over the authentication practices of other parties: “Let’s say we have a customer who we’re protecting,” explains Baggett. “They’re safe, but imagine that they start getting suspicious emails from a third party.
