Super Heavy and Ship, however, will steer themselves directly back to their launch tower, which will capture each vehicle with its "chopstick" arms. This will allow SpaceX to inspect, refurbish and refly Starship at an accelerated rate, which is a priority for the company: Musk has said he envisions launching Starship more than 10,000 times per year by 2030. Starship has conducted 14 test flights to date, and SpaceX has pulled off chopstick catches with Super Heavy on three of them. The company has not yet tried to catch Ship, which is a more difficult proposition, as the upper stage travels higher, farther and faster than the booster does. Still, Musk is confident that SpaceX will pull off a Ship catch on the first try. (He did not give a specific target date for Flight 15, saying only that it was expected next month.) "I'd say it's more likely than not that this succeeds next flight," he said. "And if not, we have a steady stream of Starship flight attempts through the end of this year, and and then accelerating next year." Success would mean back-to-back Starship flights with huge milestones. On Flight 14, which occurred on Sept. 28, Ship reached orbit for the first time ever . It also deployed 26 of SpaceX's Starlink Version 3 satellites — the first 26 members of a next-gen broadband constellation in low Earth orbit that will eventually consist of about 100,000 spacecraft . The Starship Flight 15 preview was something of an aside during today's call. The event primarily served to announce SpaceX's financial performance during Q3, the three-month stretch that ended on Sept. 30. And that performance was strong, company representatives said. SpaceX recorded revenues of $14.6 billion during Q3, an increase of 161% from the $5.6 billion earned during Q3 of 2025. The company had a net income of $4.4 billion during Q3, $5.5 billion better than the result from the same stretch last year, when SpaceX lost $1.1 billion. Just $1.8 billion of 2026 Q3 revenue came from SpaceX's launch division. The vast majority was generated by two other segments — connectivity (services provided by its Starlink megaconstellation) and artificial intelligence (or, as the Trump administration has recently rebranded it, "superintelligence"). SpaceX thinks these latter two segments will continue to boom. That's why it's building the infrastructure to support thousands of Starship launches per year — to loft lots of Starlink satellites and AI data centers to Earth orbit. And the company believes that it's positioned to really start raking in the cash, starting as soon as next year. "In a nutshell, what this implies for SpaceX annual recurring revenue by the end of '27 is somewhere between 500 billion [dollars] and a trillion," Musk said.

item.title: Auto tech startup claims it traced hack attempt back to rival's IP address
item.description: An automotive tech startup claims that its IT systems were attacked by individuals trying to steal its driving model, and that those attacks came from an IP address associated with a rival in the space. The tech startup, IQ.Lvbs, described the alleged security incident in a recent blog post . On October 3, IQ.Lvbs introduced the private beta of NovaSpark , the first model for the company's IQ.Pilot app, in the Comma.ai Discord channel. They put it in that channel because the model requires the use of Comma.ai's camera hardware, which is built for self-driving vehicles. From there, things got weird. "From October 7 to 14, we faced repeated attempts to steal NovaSpark, access users’ devices and private driving files, and exploit our sign-in system," the IQ.Lvbs blog post claims. "The first requests came from an IP assigned to Comma.ai Inc." In addition, on October 8 – shortly after the alleged attacks began – somebody banned IQ.Lvbs' team from the Comma.ai Discord channel. Posts on the IQ.Pilot Discord channel indicate that individuals doing private beta testing for IQ.Lvbs have also been banned from that channel. One of the three people involved in IQ.Lvbs, a UI/UX designer who asked to be identified only as "Cat," speculated to The Register about the reasons for the alleged hack and Discord ban. "Our model, NovaSpark, is a good deal ahead of Comma's latest small and large models, which directly threatens their core business of making AI models good enough to sell their hardware," he said. "Comma for the most part has been stagnant in their models' improvement and that was a main driver for us making NovaSpark." An October 7, 2026 Discord message from user Torq_boi, said to be Harald Schäfer, Comma.ai’s CTO, implies NovaSpark was distilled from Comma.ai's Rebellious Hope model. “I’m glad people are training models and experimenting with this stuff," the post starts. "But don’t lie to people about what you’re doing, and saying it’s not a finetune of existing comma models when it is. That’s not cool.” IQ.Lvbs disputes that assertion and says it did the work on its own. item.dc:creator: Thomas Claburn
item.content:encoded: An automotive tech startup claims that its IT systems were attacked by individuals trying to steal its driving model, and that those attacks came from an IP address associated with a rival in the space. The tech startup, IQ.Lvbs, described the alleged security incident in a recent blog post . On October 3, IQ.Lvbs introduced the private beta of NovaSpark , the first model for the company's IQ.Pilot app, in the Comma.ai Discord channel. They put it in that channel because the model requires the use of Comma.ai's camera hardware, which is built for self-driving vehicles. From there, things got weird. "From October 7 to 14, we faced repeated attempts to steal NovaSpark, access users’ devices and private driving files, and exploit our sign-in system," the IQ.Lvbs blog post claims. "The first requests came from an IP assigned to Comma.ai Inc." In addition, on October 8 – shortly after the alleged attacks began – somebody banned IQ.Lvbs' team from the Comma.ai Discord channel. Posts on the IQ.Pilot Discord channel indicate that individuals doing private beta testing for IQ.Lvbs have also been banned from that channel. One of the three people involved in IQ.Lvbs, a UI/UX designer who asked to be identified only as "Cat," speculated to The Register about the reasons for the alleged hack and Discord ban. "Our model, NovaSpark, is a good deal ahead of Comma's latest small and large models, which directly threatens their core business of making AI models good enough to sell their hardware," he said. "Comma for the most part has been stagnant in their models' improvement and that was a main driver for us making NovaSpark." An October 7, 2026 Discord message from user Torq_boi, said to be Harald Schäfer, Comma.ai’s CTO, implies NovaSpark was distilled from Comma.ai's Rebellious Hope model. “I’m glad people are training models and experimenting with this stuff," the post starts. "But don’t lie to people about what you’re doing, and saying it’s not a finetune of existing comma models when it is. That’s not cool.” IQ.Lvbs disputes that assertion and says it did the work on its own. "The claim that NovaSpark is Rebellious Hope with a short fine-tune and an unchanged policy does not survive scrutiny, and we’re not sure how Comma came to that conclusion, especially considering that they do not possess NovaSpark’s model weights or ONNX," the biz said. In the log data IQ.Lvbs published to support its claims, the company flags the username haraschax as one of those associated with Comma.ai IP addresses. Schäfer uses that username on GitHub. Comma.ai and Schäfer did not respond to requests for comment sent to several different addresses. The Discord user Torq_boi in the Comma.ai channel did not respond to a DM seeking comment. Comma.ai is currently being investigated [PDF] by the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration to assess whether its driving automation tech contributed to five crashes and three deaths. IQ.Lvbs says it's considering legal action over the alleged hack. "We are currently reviewing our legal options and looking into involving the authorities," said Cat. ®

item.title: On this day in space! Oct. 20, 1970: The Soviet Union launches last-ever Zond moon mission
item.description: null On Oct. 20, 1970, the Soviet Union launched the Zond 8 spacecraft on a mission to the moon. This was the last mission in the Zond program. After the first three Zond missions explored Venus and Mars , the next ones were circumlunar missions that flew around the moon before returning to Earth. Although there was no crew on board, the Zond spacecraft was designed with cosmonauts in mind. The Zond missions served as test flights for the Soviet Union's plans to send cosmonauts to the moon. But those plans for crewed flights never came to fruition. This was partly because the U.S. had already put astronauts on the moon , but also because the Zond missions had a lot of technical problems. Zond 8 was considered a success — even though its guidance system malfunctioned on the way back to Earth. The spacecraft still returned to Earth safely and splashed down in the Indian Ocean one week after it launched. The Soviet Union's Zond 8 spacecraft, the last in a series of lunar spacecraft, captured this image of Earthrise on Oct. 24, 1970. (Image credit: Moscow State University of Geodesy and Cartography) Why it mattered While the Zond 1 and Zond 2 missions were launched toward Venus and Mars, respectively, the primary target of most Zond missions was the moon. At the time, the Soviet Union was embroiled in an ongoing space race with the United States to be the first on the moon with a human crew. By the time Zond 8 launched on Oct. 20, 1970, that space race was lost to the Soviet Union. NASA and the U.S. had already landed astronauts on the moon twice with Apollo 11 and Apollo 12 (in July and November of 1969, respectively), and even peformed the first space rescue fo the Apollo 13 astronauts in April 1970. While Zond 8 was uncrewed, it was a test flight of the Soviet Union's L1 spacecraft that was designed to fly a cosmonaut around the moon. It looped around the moon in a lunar flyby, approaching within 1,120 kilometers of the moon's surface at its closest point, according to RussianSpaceWeb.com . An artist's illustration of a Zond spacecraft. (Image credit: Future) Cameras on Zond 8 captured stunning views of the Earth and moon, recreating the iconic Earthrise views seen by Apollo 8 astronauts two years earlier in 1968. Zond 8 ultimately splashed down in the Indian Ocean on Oct. 27, 1970 after a solar attitude sensor failed, sending it on a shorter, steeper reentry path during landing, according to RussianSpaceWeb.com. It was retrieved by a recovery ship, marking the end of the Soviet moon landing program. Russian would go on to develop a series of Salyut space stations , culminating in the long-lived Mir space station . After decades without a moon probe, Russia did launch a new uncrewed moon lander in 2023. That Luna 25 mission failed and crashed into the lunar surface after an onboard engine controller malfunctioned. The country has pledged a return to the moon in 2027. Want more space history? item.title: Can’t make it to the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art for the 'Star Wars' display? This is the companion book set you’re looking for!
item.description: null Taschen, purveyors of fine art and design special-edition books, have teamed up with George Lucas and his newly opened Lucas Museum of Narrative Art in Los Angeles to present a masterful two-volume catalog of the museum’s illuminating offerings. Housed in a sturdy slipcase, readers will discover a pair of lavishly illustrated volumes spanning 832 pages and tipping the scales at nearly 14 pounds. At $200 for the pair, it's not cheap, but look on the bright side; hoisting these illustrated tomes will save you a subscription to your local gym! This immersive collection documents in great detail the astounding scope of rare items on display in Lucas’s treasury of paintings, murals, photographs, sculptures, posters, comic strips, illustrations, costumes, and magazine covers that have spurred humankind’s imagination. Developed in collaboration with George Lucas and the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art, this extensive two-volume catalog brings together an unparalleled collection of narrative art. View Deal We'd absolutely recommend checking out the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art in person if you can. Our own Chelsea Gohd visited the Los Angeles-based museum ahead of its opening in September 2026 and adored it. But if you're not a California local, getting lost in this collection's glossy pages is the next best thing to roaming the museum exhibitions on a rainy afternoon. Volumes I and II of Tashen's stunning "Lucas Museum of Narrative Art" edition (Image credit: Taschen) Far beyond a mere companion to the marvels inside the fantastic spaceship-shaped building poised near the University of Southern California campus — the same institution where Lucas attended film school in the late 1960s — these bold editions are an adventure in their own right. Waiting to be absorbed is an impressive assortment of storytelling expression that showcases beautiful works by everyone from Maxfield Parrish, N.C. Wyeth, and Norman Rockwell to Frank Frazetta, Jack Kirby, and Ralph McQuarrie. Lucas and his wife, Mellody Hobson, curated the museum’s contents that represent decades of collecting narrative art in all of its forms. From Taschen's "Lucas Museum of the Narrative Art" catalog (Image credit: Taschen) Our friends at Taschen were gracious enough to send us one of these Lucas Museum of Narrative Art special editions, and in unboxing this magnificent pair of books, one can feel the quality in the deluxe binding and thick covers. Inside you’ll find an eye-popping array of full-color photography and sharp descriptions for hundreds of artworks, all hand-picked by Lucas and Hobson. Lucas himself delivers the preface, which is titled "The Art of Story," where he professes his love of art, myth, anthropology, illustrators, and cinema. He recalls when he came to meet his mentor, Professor Joseph Campbell, and how he amassed 40,000 pieces of art beginning when he was a student at USC. From Taschen's "Lucas Museum of the Narrative Art" catalog (Image credit: Taschen) The great di

Wyeth, and Norman Rockwell to Frank Frazetta, Jack Kirby, and Ralph McQuarrie. From Taschen's "Lucas Museum of the Narrative Art" catalog (Image credit: Taschen) Our friends at Taschen were gracious enough to send us one of these Lucas Museum of Narrative Art special editions, and in unboxing this magnificent pair of books, one can feel the quality in the deluxe binding and thick covers. He recalls when he came to meet his mentor, Professor Joseph Campbell, and how he amassed 40,000 pieces of art beginning when he was a student at USC. From Taschen's "Lucas Museum of the Narrative Art" catalog (Image credit: Taschen) The great director Guillermo del Toro provides a heartfelt foreword praising the importance of the museum and these prestigious companion volumes depicting a multitude of visual wonders. Between the duo of volumes, sections are divided into chapters dealing with topics such as history, children's stories, the American West, everyday life, romance and adventure, photography, science fiction and fantasy, and, of course, Star Wars in Motion. From Taschen's "Lucas Museum of the Narrative Art" catalog (Image credit: Taschen) They take you on an overwhelming journey through the gallery’s incredibly diverse holdings, not least of which are archival items and concept art chronicling Lucas's involvement in the galaxy far, far away. This remarkable " Star Wars " section will be of particular interest to sci-fi aficionados, as it contains 100 pages of original props, paintings, concept artwork, costumes, models, and digital renderings created by some of Lucasfilm and Industrial Light and Magic’s best and brightest talents. From Taschen's "Lucas Museum of the Narrative Art" catalog (Image credit: Taschen) Taken with the rest of the 832 combined pages of Taschen's ambitious release that fully captures the dizzying breadth of the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art , it's a brilliant keepsake to spark your soul and imagination. The Lucas Museum of Narrative Art two-book collection is available now via Taschen's website and Amazon . item.title: Nigeria Confirms First Ebola Case in Abuja
item.description: Following the Federal Government’s confirmation of an Ebola case in the FCT, health authorities have activated nationwide surveillance and urged the public to remain calm while strictly following official safety guidelines. The Federal Government of Nigeria has confirmed a case of the Ebola virus disease in the Federal Capital Territory (FCT), Abuja . According to an official press statement issued on October 20, 2026, and signed by the Coordinating Minister of Health and Social Welfare, Professor Muhammad Ali Pate , the patient is a woman who recently arrived in Nigeria on an international flight from Uganda . She was admitted to a private hospital in the FCT, where she received care for several days before laboratory confirmation established the diagnosis . She has since been moved to an isolation facility, where she is currently receiving medical care . In response to the development, the Federal Ministry of Health, the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control (NCDC), and the FCT Health Services Secretariat have mobilised a swift public health response to contain the spread . Contact tracing is already underway, with 44 close contacts—spanning healthcare workers, caregivers, patients, and travel companions—identified and placed under monitoring . Public health teams have also stepped up surveillance and are providing direct support to the hospital to reinforce infection prevention and control standards . Authorities have put all public and private healthcare facilities nationwide on high alert, urging medical personnel to maintain a high index of suspicion, isolate suspected cases promptly, and report them to health authorities immediately . Reassuring the public, the government noted that Nigeria successfully contained an Ebola outbreak back in 2014, building a robust public health framework and experienced response system . However, officials emphasised that safeguarding public health requires a collective effort . What Nigerians Should Know and Do Public health authorities have outlined essential guidelines to keep everyone safe while urging citizens to remain calm and avoid panic : How It Spreads: Ebola is transmitted through direct contact with the blood or body fluids of an infected person who is exhibiting symptoms or has died from the disease, as well as through contact with contaminated materials . Individuals cannot transmit the virus before symptoms manifest . Stay Calm and Vigilant: Remain composed and rely strictly on verified updates from official health bodies to curb misinformation and stigma . Practice Good Hygiene: Maintain regular hand hygiene and strictly avoid contact with the body fluids of anyone suspected of carrying the virus . Watch for Symptoms: Look out for warning signs such as sudden fever, severe weakness, headaches, vomiting, and diarrhoea, particularly if there is a history of potential exposure . item.title: Jeff Bezos is playing the long game with Blue Origin (op-ed)
item.description:
Daniel Biedermann is a Partner at NewSpace Capital, a private equity firm investing in high-growth space companies. He has more than 30 years' experience in the space industry and was previously SVP of Corporate Strategy at SES, where he played a leading role in acquisitions and the creation of joint ventures, including LuxGovSat. Before joining SES, he held engineering and mission management roles at Arianespace and Contraves Space, working on more than 40 space and launch missions.

Daniel Biedermann is a partner at NewSpace Capital. He contributed this article to Space.com's Expert Voices: Op-Ed & Insights . Jeff Bezos , the founder and former CEO of Amazon, recently said that Blue Origin , his space technology company, is likely to go public in the coming years. The announcement has (unsurprisingly) attracted considerable attention, not least because Bezos has spent more than two decades financing the company largely from his personal wealth. He has invested billions of dollars in developing rockets , spacecraft and other forms of technology, often with very little prospect of an immediate return. But although Bezos has now raised the possibility of an initial public offering, he has given no firm indication of when one might happen. He may be right to keep his options open. Bezos founded Blue Origin in 2000. Because he has financed so much of its development by himself , the company has been able to pursue ambitious engineering projects without the financial pressures that publicly listed businesses typically face. But developing reusable rockets, manufacturing spacecraft and building the infrastructure needed for future lunar missions requires extraordinary amounts of capital: These projects can take decades to complete, and even the wealthiest investors must think hard about how best to finance them over the long term. Bezos, then, has good reasons to seek additional sources of investment — particularly as Blue Origin prepares to expand its commercial operations. An IPO would give Blue Origin the means to raise substantial capital from public investors and reduce its dependence on Bezos's personal wealth. The company could then use that money to expand manufacturing, develop new technology and compete for a greater share of the growing space market. Public ownership would also give existing investors the power to sell some of their holdings and could make it easier for Blue Origin to finance acquisitions. But the company would also have to meet the expectations of shareholders, who would expect to see regular evidence of commercial progress. This, I suspect, is why Bezos wants to establish a stronger business before committing to a listing. It might have much to prove commercially, but Blue Origin’s technical progress has been remarkable. item.content:encoded:
Daniel Biedermann is a Partner at NewSpace Capital, a private equity firm investing in high-growth space companies. He has more than 30 years' experience in the space industry and was previously SVP of Corporate Strategy at SES, where he played a leading role in acquisitions and the creation of joint ventures, including LuxGovSat. Before joining SES, he held engineering and mission management roles at Arianespace and Contraves Space, working on more than 40 space and launch missions.

Daniel Biedermann is a partner at NewSpace Capital. He contributed this article to Space.com's Expert Voices: Op-Ed & Insights . Jeff Bezos , the founder and former CEO of Amazon, recently said that Blue Origin , his space technology company, is likely to go public in the coming years. The announcement has (unsurprisingly) attracted considerable attention, not least because Bezos has spent more than two decades financing the company largely from his personal wealth. He has invested billions of dollars in developing rockets , spacecraft and other forms of technology, often with very little prospect of an immediate return. But although Bezos has now raised the possibility of an initial public offering, he has given no firm indication of when one might happen. He may be right to keep his options open. Bezos founded Blue Origin in 2000. Because he has financed so much of its development by himself , the company has been able to pursue ambitious engineering projects without the financial pressures that publicly listed businesses typically face. But developing reusable rockets, manufacturing spacecraft and building the infrastructure needed for future lunar missions requires extraordinary amounts of capital: These projects can take decades to complete, and even the wealthiest investors must think hard about how best to finance them over the long term. Bezos, then, has good reasons to seek additional sources of investment — particularly as Blue Origin prepares to expand its commercial operations. An IPO would give Blue Origin the means to raise substantial capital from public investors and reduce its dependence on Bezos's personal wealth. The company could then use that money to expand manufacturing, develop new technology and compete for a greater share of the growing space market. Public ownership would also give existing investors the power to sell some of their holdings and could make it easier for Blue Origin to finance acquisitions. But the company would also have to meet the expectations of shareholders, who would expect to see regular evidence of commercial progress. This, I suspect, is why Bezos wants to establish a stronger business before committing to a listing. It might have much to prove commercially, but Blue Origin’s technical progress has been remarkable. In January 2025, its New Glenn rocket reached orbit for the first time — a significant achievement for a vehicle built to compete in the heavy-lift launch market. The company has also secured government and commercial contracts and continued developing its lunar capabilities. But it will eventually have to demonstrate that it can launch New Glenn frequently, reliably and at a commercially competitive cost, and it is still some way away from that point. Some will be asking whether Bezos wants to raise money to accelerate growth or simply to reduce the amount he himself must invest. Such doubts could affect the company's valuation and make it harder to attract investors who share its long-term ambitions. But again, this suggests Bezos is playing the long game. And given the enthusiasm that has surrounded some billionaire-led space ventures, this is sensible. Investors have sometimes attached extraordinary valuations to companies with ambitious plans but limited commercial experience. Space businesses certainly require ambition: engineers will often spend years developing technology before they can sell it. But investors have to distinguish between technical achievement and commercial performance. At the end of the day, they are seeking a strong rate of return. Blue Origin's New Glenn rocket launches NASA's ESCAPADE Mars mission on Nov. 13, 2025. (Image credit: Blue Origin) What’s also worth considering is how Blue Origin's progress could benefit the wider space industry, particularly the specialist companies that supply technology to larger manufacturers and operators. SpaceX has achieved remarkable success in part by developing and manufacturing much of its technology internally. This includes its rockets, spacecraft and satellites . Blue Origin also does something similar, undertaking substantial engineering and manufacturing work itself, but it is not quite so vertically integrated, and thus may have greater scope to work with external suppliers as it expands. It already buys parts, equipment and services from hundreds of businesses. If it can successfully increase its production and launch activity, these suppliers could receive more orders and gain opportunities to develop new technologies. That’s to the good of the sector as a whole. Why? Because a successful space industry needs more than a handful of large launch providers. It needs companies specializing in satellite communications, propulsion, electronics, software and other areas. Such businesses may have developed highly sophisticated products, but they need bigger customers and predictable demand to expand and produce more. Blue Origin could become an important customer for some of these, particularly if it chooses to buy specialist technology rather than make everything internally. Greater competition between the bigger space companies could translate to more potential customers for suppliers and fewer dependent commercial relationships. Investors would benefit. There’s real potential in businesses that provide the technology and services on which larger space companies depend — the ‘picks and shovels.’ These can sometimes serve several customers and markets, making them less dependent on the success of a single program. A growing Blue Origin would create more opportunities for companies like these — although, of course, much will depend on how Bezos chooses to organize its supply chain. We shouldn’t assume that Blue Origin will become more open to external suppliers than its competitors, but the possibility is at least worth entertaining. As it is, Bezos still faces substantial challenges. Blue Origin is not yet a commercially mature business. The company must increase its launch activity; it must demonstrate its reliability; and it must compete for customers in the public and private sectors. It must also decide how much technology to manufacture internally and whether and where third parties can provide better products or products at a lower cost. Bezos has the resources to give the company time to answer these questions, and he appears to be willing to use them. If he continues to prioritize commercial performance before pursuing an IPO, then Blue Origin could eventually enter the public markets in a much stronger position.

item.title: Folorunso Alakija Receives Honorary Doctorate From UK’s University of Buckingham
item.description: Folorunso Alakija with Vice-Chancellor Professor David Cole at the University of Buckingham. From fashion and banking to oil and gas, Nigerian businesswoman and philanthropist Folorunso Alakija has built a career across several industries. Now, the University of Buckingham in the United Kingdom has recognised her achievements with an honorary doctorate, celebrating her contributions to business, philanthropy and society. The honour was conferred on Friday, 16 October 2026, at the university’s Radcliffe Centre during Buckingham Africa Day, as the institution marked its 50th anniversary. Dressed in a red doctoral gown, Alakija received the degree from Vice-Chancellor Professor David Cole , with family, friends and members of the university community in attendance. For Alakija, the occasion was also an opportunity to speak to the next generation about ambition, responsibility and the importance of creating opportunities for others. Folorunso Alakija in her doctoral gown at the University of Buckingham conferment ceremony. Accepting the honorary degree, she thanked God and the university for the recognition, sharing her belief in Africa’s potential and the responsibility that comes with achievement. “Africa is a continent of immense potential, creativity and resilience and that achievement carries responsibility to serve others,” she said. She also encouraged students and young people to pursue their goals with passion, perseverance and diligence, while remaining humble and recognising the value of their contributions. Her message reflects a career that has taken her through several fields. Before becoming widely known for her work in oil and gas through Famfa Oil, Alakija worked in banking and established herself in Nigeria’s fashion industry. Folorunso Alakija with Dean of Faculty Professor Debarpita Bardhan-Correia at the Radcliffe Centre. item.title: A supercomputer is about to launch to the moon aboard a rover named FLIP
item.description: null HAWTHORNE, Calif. — A moon buggy carrying a history-making supercomputer is ready to launch to the lunar surface. And it's taking some inspiration from Mars. Later this year, Astrolab will launch its uncrewed moon rover FLIP to the lunar south pole as part of the Griffin Mission 1, or Griffin-1. The California company is one of two that NASA has selected to develop a drivable rover for the agency's Artemis program. On board FLIP will be Hewlett Packard Enterprise's (HPE) Spaceborne Computer-4, an advanced computer module built to be used in space. This will be the first time that high-performance computing and artificial intelligence will be tested on the lunar surface. As NASA gets closer to landing humans back on the moon with Artemis, advancements like this aim to support future human habitation as well as economic activity on and around the moon. "We're sending the first supercomputer from HPE to the lunar surface later this year, doing the first GPU [graphics processing unit] on the moon [and the] first AI experiments on the moon," Jaret Matthews, founder and CEO of Astrolab, said during an Oct. 14 media event here at Astrolab's headquarters. "They're breaking new ground, and they're ahead of the curve." The computer is designed to be lightweight, compact, self-contained and fanless. It has a low-power 64-bit CPU (central processing unit) with a GPU. The computer will be attached to FLIP's cooling system and will be powered by a system supported by both batteries and solar cells on the rover. The computer will also be paired with solid state drives from the company KIOXIA that will allow for memory storage. Mission Control at Astrolab. Chelsea Gohd Astrolab CEO and founder Jaret Matthews points out the Astrolab landing site among other locations at the lunar south pole. Chelsea Gohd Jaret Matthews presents Astrolab's FLIP rover. Chelsea Gohd The FLIP rover's headlights and attached artwork. Chelsea Gohd A close-up of the attached artwork on the FLIP rover. Chelsea Gohd So, what will a supercomputer and AI accomplish on this uncrewed mission? First and foremost, the flightwill test how the computer works in this extreme environment. The computer is built with heat-conductive aluminum and is designed with the specific conditions of the lunar south pole in mind. But while it was designed and tested to be able to withstand the extreme temperatures and conditions on the moon's surface, the upcoming mission seeks to show that this advanced technology can actually work in this environment. "NASA's given us a real challenge," Matthews told Space.com at the media event. "We have to design for a full year on the lunar surface. So that means surviving multiple lunar nights, upwards of 150 hours of complete darkness where we're not receiving energy or warmth from the sun. And then, also, there's going to be a long period [in] which we're operating semi-autonomously for [when] the astronauts are not there … and so we're having to develop a semi-auto

item.content:encoded: null HAWTHORNE, Calif. — A moon buggy carrying a history-making supercomputer is ready to launch to the lunar surface. And it's taking some inspiration from Mars. Later this year, Astrolab will launch its uncrewed moon rover FLIP to the lunar south pole as part of the Griffin Mission 1, or Griffin-1. The California company is one of two that NASA has selected to develop a drivable rover for the agency's Artemis program. On board FLIP will be Hewlett Packard Enterprise's (HPE) Spaceborne Computer-4, an advanced computer module built to be used in space. This will be the first time that high-performance computing and artificial intelligence will be tested on the lunar surface. As NASA gets closer to landing humans back on the moon with Artemis, advancements like this aim to support future human habitation as well as economic activity on and around the moon. "We're sending the first supercomputer from HPE to the lunar surface later this year, doing the first GPU [graphics processing unit] on the moon [and the] first AI experiments on the moon," Jaret Matthews, founder and CEO of Astrolab, said during an Oct. 14 media event here at Astrolab's headquarters. "They're breaking new ground, and they're ahead of the curve." The computer is designed to be lightweight, compact, self-contained and fanless. It has a low-power 64-bit CPU (central processing unit) with a GPU. The computer will be attached to FLIP's cooling system and will be powered by a system supported by both batteries and solar cells on the rover. The computer will also be paired with solid state drives from the company KIOXIA that will allow for memory storage. Mission Control at Astrolab. Chelsea Gohd Astrolab CEO and founder Jaret Matthews points out the Astrolab landing site among other locations at the lunar south pole. Chelsea Gohd Jaret Matthews presents Astrolab's FLIP rover. Chelsea Gohd The FLIP rover's headlights and attached artwork. Chelsea Gohd A close-up of the attached artwork on the FLIP rover. Chelsea Gohd So, what will a supercomputer and AI accomplish on this uncrewed mission? First and foremost, the flightwill test how the computer works in this extreme environment. The computer is built with heat-conductive aluminum and is designed with the specific conditions of the lunar south pole in mind. But while it was designed and tested to be able to withstand the extreme temperatures and conditions on the moon's surface, the upcoming mission seeks to show that this advanced technology can actually work in this environment. "NASA's given us a real challenge," Matthews told Space.com at the media event. "We have to design for a full year on the lunar surface. So that means surviving multiple lunar nights, upwards of 150 hours of complete darkness where we're not receiving energy or warmth from the sun. And then, also, there's going to be a long period [in] which we're operating semi-autonomously for [when] the astronauts are not there … and so we're having to develop a semi-autonomous platform that will spend many months [and] travel hundreds of kilometers [on the moon]." But the computer will more than just prove its durability, if all goes to plan. It will also analyze visual data captured on the mission and enable autonomous observations, process navigation, mapping and terrain analysis. The mission also promises to test AI capabilities, though it's unclear what exact applications we'll see with this lunar AI. HPE shared in a statement that "an AI services container will demonstrate reliable deployment of scalable AI service applications on the moon." It is also to be determined exactly how, once tested, these capabilities might be used with future crewed missions. Astronauts aboard the International Space Station already use computers for communications, science experiments and other daily tasks while living in space, but we can't say yet exactly how future astronauts might use these capabilities, especially with the addition of AI, on the moon. From Mars to the moon One interesting aspect of this new development is where it came from. While HPE has provided computing power to NASA for decades, Matthews is also bringing his previous experience working at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) into this new venture. "One of the experiments [that will be] running on the spaceborne computer on the moon is a localization software experiment from JPL. It has been used on Mars, and this will be the first time it's used on the moon," Matthews said. "The challenge with the moon and Mars is that there's no GPS, so locating yourself and knowing where you are on the surface [can be difficult]," he added. "So we're going to be running what is essentially a machine learning algorithm that JPL developed to take a map that's stored in memory … and compare it to the local terrain we see around us, and then do a match. So essentially, match features of the local terrain to the map that's stored in memory to help find ourselves on the map and keep ourselves away from dangerous craters." As its name suggests, Griffin-1 will be the first mission for the robotic Griffin moon lander, which was developed by Astrobotic. The Pittsburgh company is flying Griffin-1 for NASA, under the agency's CLPS (Commercial Lunar Payload Services) program. In addition to FLIP, the mission will carry Astrobiotic's CubeRover, a small, uncrewed rover; LandCam-X, an optical navigation system; and Nanofiche GLPH (Galactic Library to Preserve Humanity), a tiny archive of human history, to the moon's surface. "The moon presents a challenging environment for advanced computing, and we’re pleased to provide HPE with an opportunity to demonstrate its technology on the lunar surface," Matthews added in a statement. "Our FLIP rover is designed to accommodate a variety of payloads, and this mission will demonstrate how commercial lunar mobility platforms can support technology development and scientific research."

item.title: Talks Around Contour: Have You Met the New ZARON Contour Stick Yet?
item.description: Okay ladies, gather around because there is something to talk about! You know that moment when your makeup is looking good, but you just want a little extra definition? A little cheekbone action? A little sculpted-but-still-natural magic? You get the gist! Well, ZARON Cosmetics might just have something for you: the new ZARON Contour Stick ! And before you ask, we are talking about the kind of product that lets you decide how snatched you want your look to be. Soft glam today? Full glam tomorrow? The choice is yours! First Things First, Why a Contour Stick? Let’s be honest. Contouring can sometimes feel like a whole mathematics exam. Where exactly do you apply it? How much is too much? And why does blending sometimes feel like a workout? The struggle is real! That’s why a contour product that makes the process feel easier deserves a little attention. The ZARON Contour Stick is designed to sculpt, define, and enhance your features without making your makeup routine unnecessarily complicated. Think of it as another tool in your beauty bag for creating the look you want, whether you’re getting ready for a casual outing, a date night, or that event where you need your pictures to come out looking extra good. Wait, There’s More! Let’s Talk About the Formula Now, here’s where things get interesting. The ZARON Contour Stick is creamy, blendable, and buildable. Three words every contour lover wants to hear! Creamy? Everyone loves a product that glides onto the skin. Blendable? Because nobody is trying to walk around with harsh contour lines announcing themselves before we do! The formula is designed to blend seamlessly for a natural-looking finish without that cakey feel. Buildable? Now we’re talking! Some days, you want just a little definition. Other days, you’re going all out with the sculpted glam. This contour stick lets you build your desired level of definition with every swipe. In other words, you don’t have to commit to one look. Start soft, blend it out, and build up if you want more drama. Your face, your rules! Fall, Spring or Autumn? Pick Your Shade! You know what can make or break your contour look? Finding a shade that works for your complexion and the kind of definition you’re going for. The ZARON Contour Stick comes in three shades: Fall, Spring and Autumn. Whether you’re keeping things subtle or going for a more defined finish, these options give you room to explore your preferred contour look. And please, don’t be afraid to experiment! Makeup is supposed to be fun. Try your shade, blend it out, see how it works with your foundation, and find the finish that makes you feel your best. There’s a Little Story Behind This Launch! Here’s a detail we love: the ZARON Contour Stick was inspired by feedback from the brand’s beauty community, affectionately known as Zaronistas. item.title: BOLD ’98 Irish Whiskey Launches in Nigeria With “Party Like It’s ’98” Lagos Experience
item.description: What happens when Irish whiskey meets ’90s nostalgia, Lagos nightlife and a room full of people ready to have a good time? For BOLD ’98 Irish Whiskey , the answer was “Party Like It’s ’98” , an immersive experience that marked the brand’s formal Nigerian launch at Nomaada Restaurant in Victoria Island, Lagos. Bringing together celebrities, media personalities, distributors, tastemakers and industry stakeholders, the evening moved beyond the conventional whiskey launch format, creating an experience built around music, food, cocktails, fashion, storytelling and, naturally, whiskey. But there was something particularly interesting about the choice of theme. The ’80s, ’90s and early-2000s-inspired direction was not created as a reaction to the current nostalgia wave dominating social media and popular culture. The consumer strategy had been developed and concluded months before the event. By the time BOLD ’98 brought the concept to life in Lagos, retro culture had become increasingly visible everywhere, making the brand’s choice of direction feel almost like a glimpse into the future. L-R Kelvin Orogun, Board Chairman, Jambitts Limited; Ita Ntekim, CEO, Miami Escape; Olajumoke Oladimeji, CEO, Capston Bee; Motunrayo Raheem, Executive Director, Commercial Operations, Stafford Irish Spirits/Jambitts Limited; Kelechi Obichendu, CEO, Simple Life; and Chris Obihai, Board Chairman, Jambitts Limited. When Strategy Meets Culture For BOLD ’98, nostalgia was never simply about dressing up a premium Irish whiskey launch in old-school aesthetics. The thinking was to create an experience that would make the brand’s heritage feel relevant, familiar and culturally engaging to Nigerian consumers. “Our theme for BOLD ’98 was going to be old school, the ’90s, the ritual vibes, everything that makes you remember where you’re coming from,” said Motunrayo Raheem, Executive Director, Commercial Operations, Stafford Irish Spirits/Jambitts. The result was a Lagos whiskey experience that invited people to participate rather than simply watch. Guests captured their own Polaroid ‘’98 moments’, explored a Cocktail Lab, enjoyed food and whiskey pairings, and experienced a chef’s table curated by Nomaada. There was also a fireside conversation hosted by Zion Rufus , a staged bottle reveal, a catwalk featuring retro-inspired props, live performances and a spirited Gen-Z versus Millennial rap and dance battle. It was nostalgic, but it was also distinctly Lagos. A Whiskey With a Story Behind the party is a whiskey whose story stretches much further back than the 1990s. BOLD ’98 Irish Whiskey draws inspiration from the 1798 uprising in Ireland and the story of the pikemen of Wexford, whose fight for liberty became part of the brand’s heritage narrative. The story includes the image of barley from the rebels’ pockets sprouting on the battlefield after the fighting at Vinegar Hill, a powerful symbol of hope emerging from loss. item.content:encoded: What happens when Irish whiskey meets ’90s nostalgia, Lagos nightlife and a room full of people ready to have a good time? For BOLD ’98 Irish Whiskey , the answer was “Party Like It’s ’98” , an immersive experience that marked the brand’s formal Nigerian launch at Nomaada Restaurant in Victoria Island, Lagos. Bringing together celebrities, media personalities, distributors, tastemakers and industry stakeholders, the evening moved beyond the conventional whiskey launch format, creating an experience built around music, food, cocktails, fashion, storytelling and, naturally, whiskey. But there was something particularly interesting about the choice of theme. The ’80s, ’90s and early-2000s-inspired direction was not created as a reaction to the current nostalgia wave dominating social media and popular culture. The consumer strategy had been developed and concluded months before the event. By the time BOLD ’98 brought the concept to life in Lagos, retro culture had become increasingly visible everywhere, making the brand’s choice of direction feel almost like a glimpse into the future. L-R Kelvin Orogun, Board Chairman, Jambitts Limited; Ita Ntekim, CEO, Miami Escape; Olajumoke Oladimeji, CEO, Capston Bee; Motunrayo Raheem, Executive Director, Commercial Operations, Stafford Irish Spirits/Jambitts Limited; Kelechi Obichendu, CEO, Simple Life; and Chris Obihai, Board Chairman, Jambitts Limited. When Strategy Meets Culture For BOLD ’98, nostalgia was never simply about dressing up a premium Irish whiskey launch in old-school aesthetics. The thinking was to create an experience that would make the brand’s heritage feel relevant, familiar and culturally engaging to Nigerian consumers. “Our theme for BOLD ’98 was going to be old school, the ’90s, the ritual vibes, everything that makes you remember where you’re coming from,” said Motunrayo Raheem, Executive Director, Commercial Operations, Stafford Irish Spirits/Jambitts. The result was a Lagos whiskey experience that invited people to participate rather than simply watch. Guests captured their own Polaroid ‘’98 moments’, explored a Cocktail Lab, enjoyed food and whiskey pairings, and experienced a chef’s table curated by Nomaada. There was also a fireside conversation hosted by Zion Rufus , a staged bottle reveal, a catwalk featuring retro-inspired props, live performances and a spirited Gen-Z versus Millennial rap and dance battle. It was nostalgic, but it was also distinctly Lagos. A Whiskey With a Story Behind the party is a whiskey whose story stretches much further back than the 1990s. BOLD ’98 Irish Whiskey draws inspiration from the 1798 uprising in Ireland and the story of the pikemen of Wexford, whose fight for liberty became part of the brand’s heritage narrative. The story includes the image of barley from the rebels’ pockets sprouting on the battlefield after the fighting at Vinegar Hill, a powerful symbol of hope emerging from loss. That heritage is reflected in BOLD ’98’s philosophy: “ Rooted in Courage .” It is a story that connects Ireland’s history with a broader idea of resilience, determination, and the belief that something meaningful can emerge from adversity. For Raheem, that connection resonates strongly with Nigeria. “BOLD ’98 is rooted in bold characters and in the belief that something good can come from defiance. Nigerians will recognize that spirit, because it’s how many of us have built our own lives and businesses.” The result is an Irish whiskey brand whose story travels beyond its origins in Ireland to connect with a new generation of Nigerian consumers. Experience Before Explanation The Lagos launch was also a reflection of how BOLD ’98 intends to introduce itself to the Nigerian market. Rather than relying solely on a product presentation, the brand allowed guests to encounter the whiskey organically throughout the evening. As Raheem explained: “A whiskey is best introduced by tasting it, in good company, and not by telling people about it. We wanted the trade and consumers to feel the brand before they hear our pitch.” BOLD ’98 is a premium blended Irish whiskey with roots in County Wexford, Ireland, made from a blend of grain, pot still and malt whiskeys. The whiskey is characterized by a creamy, smooth profile with notes of caramel and toasted oak, and can be enjoyed neat, on the rocks or as part of a cocktail. At the Lagos launch, that versatility came to life through cocktails, food pairings and shared drinking occasions designed to introduce guests to the character of the whiskey rather than simply tell them about it. Why Nigeria? BOLD ’98 enters a Nigerian premium spirits market where consumers are increasingly exposed to international whiskey brands and have developed more discerning expectations around what they drink. For a new Irish whiskey in Nigeria, simply being an imported spirit is not enough. Consumers want quality, character, provenance and a story they can connect with. “Nigeria is one of the most exciting consumer markets in the world, and Nigerians have a discerning palate,” Raheem said. “They do not just want a famous name; they want quality, character and a brand with something to say.” That thinking shaped the Nigerian launch. The strategy was to create something consumers could taste, photograph, talk about, share and remember. And with Nigeria’s growing premium drinking culture, Lagos provided a natural setting for a brand that wants to sit at the intersection of Irish whiskey heritage and contemporary Nigerian culture. From 1798 to ’98 There was a fitting connection between the brand’s Irish heritage and its Nigerian launch. A whiskey inspired by a story from 1798 arrived in Lagos through a celebration centred on ’98, creating a bridge between historical heritage and contemporary culture. “Party Like It’s ’98” was ultimately more than a launch party. It was BOLD ’98’s first major statement about how it intends to show up in Nigeria: rooted in heritage, but expressed through contemporary culture, music, food, fashion and shared experiences. For Raheem, however, the ambition extends well beyond the launch night. “ Our promise with BOLD ’98 is simple. As a whiskey brand with a real Irish story, made with care and meant to be shared, we came to Nigeria to stay, and we are only getting started.” Where to Buy BOLD ’98 Irish Whiskey in Nigeria BOLD ’98 Irish Whiskey is available through selected retail stores, liquor outlets and HORECA locations across Nigeria. Consumers can also order BOLD ’98 online through participating Nigerian e-commerce and drinks platforms, including Drinks.ng . Order BOLD ’98 online: BOLD ’98 Irish Whiskey With its combination of Irish heritage, a distinctive brand story and a contemporary approach to whiskey culture, BOLD ’98 is positioning itself as more than another premium Irish whiskey in Nigeria . It has arrived with a story to tell, a culture to participate in, and an experience to build. BOLD ’98 Irish Whiskey has arrived in Nigeria, and the party is just beginning. item.title: BEYOND on Tour V: Redefining Rest, Recovery and the Future of African Wellness
item.description: From its signature Sunset Ride at Lakowe Lakes to personalised recovery experiences and dermatological skincare innovation, BEYOND Fitness Africa is creating a new expression of wellness rooted in movement, culture and community. The experience includes personalised IV infusions, full-body massages, assisted stretching, breathwork, recovery treatments and specialist wellness consultations, alongside thoughtfully curated dining and entertainment. Movement enthusiasts can enjoy Sunrise Sculpt, Aqua Conditioning, golf, mobility and Total Body Strength with adidas OG Sport. Aquafina, the Official Hydration Partner, supports guests throughout the programme. Beyond physical wellbeing, Mrs Ifeoma Monye will lead Pretty Balancing Act: Creating a Life System That Works , an insightful conversation on creating practical systems that support personal wellbeing, professional ambitions and the demands of everyday life. A highlight of the weekend is the return of the signature Sunset Ride, featuring a live performance by Loud Urban Choir beside the lake. Guests can also enjoy the performance from La Roche-Posay’s Sunset Viewing Lounge. The evening continues with Filmhouse After Dark, featuring karaoke, barbecue and cinema under the stars. BYD joins as Official Mobility Partner, while Instax, the Official Memory Partner, captures moments from the weekend. Together, these experiences bring BEYOND’s approach to movement, restoration and community to life. La Roche-Posay Brings Skin Health into the Wellness Experience As Official Dermatological Skincare Partner, La Roche-Posay will introduce a dedicated Skin Studio, offering guests one-to-one dermatologist consultations, personalised skincare education and practical sun protection guidance. The brand will also present Sunrise Sculpt, integrating skin health awareness into outdoor movement. For Williams, the collaboration reflects the importance of looking at wellbeing more holistically. “Wellbeing goes beyond exercise. It’s about understanding how different aspects of our health work together. Our partnership with La Roche-Posay brings skin health into that conversation, giving guests access to specialist knowledge they can apply in their everyday lives.” Beyond the Retreat: La Roche-Posay Living Lab Opens in Lagos Just days after BEYOND on Tour V, La Roche-Posay will bring its Living Lab to Victoria Island, Lagos, on 5 and 6 November 2026. The immersive public experience will bring together scientists, dermatologists, patients and consumers to explore skincare innovation and encourage meaningful conversations around skin health. Visitors will journey through five interactive stages: Discover, Test, Experience, Learn and Consult. The experience will feature Innovation Corners dedicated to La Roche-Posay’s Effaclar, Anthelios, Mela B3, Cicaplast and Lipikar ranges, alongside the LRP Café, expert discussions, the Scars of Life Cinema and professional skincare consultations. Designed to make dermatological science more accessible, Living Lab places real-life experiences and individual needs at the centre of skincare education and innovation. The event will take place at Plots 8 and 9, Ligali Ayorinde Street, beside GAC Motors, Victoria Island, Lagos, from 9 am to 7 pm on both days. Visitors can reserve their places at www.livinglabnigeria.com Building the Future of African Wellness For BEYOND Fitness Africa, its fifth destination retreat represents another step towards building a wellness brand with relevance and reach beyond Lagos. By combining premium fitness and recovery experiences with African music, culture, hospitality and specialist partnerships, BEYOND is demonstrating the potential for world-class wellness experiences created on the continent. As Williams puts it: “Africa has an incredible opportunity to shape the future of wellness. We have the creativity, talent, culture and a growing audience that understands the importance of investing in their wellbeing. Our ambition is to continue raising the standard of wellness experiences here while building a brand that helps people feel, function and live better.” As BEYOND on Tour enters its fifth edition, its message is simple: wellness is not only about how far we can push ourselves, but also about how intentionally we recover and care for ourselves along the way. item.title: The dangers of letting tech billionaires shape our world
item.description: As SpaceX impacts Ukraine and AI-generated music divides artists and fans, critics are asking what happens when technology has too much control over our lives This was originally published in TechScape, a newsletter about how technology shapes our lives. Sign up to receive it here Hello, and welcome to TechScape. I’m Blake Montgomery, US tech editor at the Guardian, writing to you while sitting in front of Roy Lichtenstein’s monumental Drowning Girl, on view in New York City . Today in tech, we’re discussing the perils of Elon Musk’s one-man global infrastructure, AI-generated music and a Guardian AI conference in Paris. Continue reading...

item.title: Labor and the Coalition are poised to take a reckless gamble on AI. Haven’t they realised community support has collapsed? | Edward Santow and Sarah Sacher
item.description: Australian workers expect the government to act to protect them from AI harms. There is a clear reform solution at hand Get our new political email , free app or daily news podcast Australia’s major political parties are edging towards rare consensus. Labor and the Coalition increasingly want to take a major bet on artificial intelligence. Yet, just as the parties are coming together, the Australian community is running the other way. Last year, only 30% of Australians believed the benefits of AI outweighed the risks. In 2026, community trust in AI appears to be falling even further. Continue reading...

item.title: The view from the edge of a sparkling spiral galaxy | Space photo of the day for Oct. 20, 2026
item.description: null The spiral galaxy NGC 1827, as seen from the side by the Hubble Space Telescope. (Image credit: NASA, ESA, Michael Jones (California Institute of Technology); Image Processing: Gladys Kober (NASA/Catholic University of America)) If you were approaching the edge of a spiral galaxy, arriving from afar through the cosmos, it might look something like this. What is it? In this new snapshot by the Hubble Space Telescope 's Advanced Camera for Surveys (ACS), we can see the edge of the spiral galaxy NGC 1827. Found about 37 million light-years from Earth, this galaxy sparkles in this side-on view. Not all spiral galaxies are the same. This galaxy is what is known as an "intermediate" spiral, which means that its structure sits somewhere between that of a barred and unbarred spiral galaxy. Barred galaxies have a distinctive central, bar-shaped structure, while the unbarred variety lacks this bar and can look more like circular spirals. NGC 1827's spiral shape isn't clear from the side, however. From this perspective, we see its twinkling edge, speckled with stars and woven together with brown ribbons of dust. Why is it incredible? Beneath the beauty of this spiral edge lies an expansive, cosmic landscape. Bright blue stars dot the spiral's side, with one particularly luminous star taking the spotlight with four diffraction spikes — created by light bending through the inner workings of Hubble's camera — emanating from its center. This image was captured as part of a larger Hubble survey that's exploring 260 satellite galaxies, which are galaxies gravitationally bound to larger hosts. Hubble is specifically looking to survey satellite galaxies that lie near host galaxies similar to our own Milky Way . So far, Hubble has spotted 111 such satellites and will continue to observe, hunting for the rest. By studying satellite galaxies like this one, which also happens to be an especially low-mass galaxy, researchers could better understand the complicated dynamics both within the galaxies themselves and between them and their host galaxies.

item.title: Red light, white light: How to preserve your night vision while using stargazing apps
item.description: The best stargazing apps can take your observation of the night sky to the next level, whether that's using augmented reality (AR mode) to identify stars or looking up the next lunar eclipse . However, the bright light emitted by smartphone screens can prevent your eyes from adjusting to the dark. If you're using one of the best telescopes , you'll want to preserve your night vision even more. Fortunately, there are ways to all but eliminate this problem. Why are bright screens bad for stargazing? The brighter your screen, the harder you'll find it to spot distant objects in the night sky. (Image credit: Getty Images) When you step out into the dark, it can take up to 20-30 minutes for your vision to adjust. The rod cells in your eyes build up a chemical known as rhodopsin, which gives you night vision. However, bright light bleaches that chemical, negatively impacting your night vision. So when you look through a telescope, binoculars or just turn your eyes to the night sky after peering at a bright phone screen, it'll be harder for you to pick out fainter objects such as galaxies and nebulas. One way of fixing this problem is simply to put your phone away and wait another 20-30 minutes. But if you're using a stargazing app to help you navigate the night skies, that's not really an option. The good news is that, between individual stargazing apps and your phone's own built-in features, you can minimize the impact of your smartphone's screen light. How to block white light in stargazing apps SkyView and several other stargazing apps let you apply a red filter. (Image credit: Skyview) Many of the best stargazing apps will let you enable a red light filter or similar, though this option may not always be present in the free version. Here's how to do that in three of our favorite stargazing apps: SkyView : Tap the screen, tap the horizontal lines, tap on Settings, then Display, then Night Mode and Red. Star Walk 2 : Tap the horizontal lines, tap on Settings, then tap the button next to Night Mode. Sky Tonight: Tap the horizontal lines, tap on Settings, then Tools, then Night Mode. All these modes will minimize the amount of white light coming from the app. However, be aware that this is only within the app. Once you go back to your phone's main menu, it will be at full color. With the red screen naturally looking darker, you may have turned up the brightness on your phone, so making the switch away from the app will be quite the shock. If you want to dim your whole phone or put it into red light mode, here's how to do that on Android or iPhone . How to block white light on Android phones Many Android phones, including recent Pixel and Samsung models, include the equivalent of a red filter. (Image credit: Samsung) On Android, there are several ways to minimize the impact of bright light, depending on the model and make of phone you have. item.content:encoded: The best stargazing apps can take your observation of the night sky to the next level, whether that's using augmented reality (AR mode) to identify stars or looking up the next lunar eclipse . However, the bright light emitted by smartphone screens can prevent your eyes from adjusting to the dark. If you're using one of the best telescopes , you'll want to preserve your night vision even more. Fortunately, there are ways to all but eliminate this problem. Why are bright screens bad for stargazing? The brighter your screen, the harder you'll find it to spot distant objects in the night sky. (Image credit: Getty Images) When you step out into the dark, it can take up to 20-30 minutes for your vision to adjust. The rod cells in your eyes build up a chemical known as rhodopsin, which gives you night vision. However, bright light bleaches that chemical, negatively impacting your night vision. So when you look through a telescope, binoculars or just turn your eyes to the night sky after peering at a bright phone screen, it'll be harder for you to pick out fainter objects such as galaxies and nebulas. One way of fixing this problem is simply to put your phone away and wait another 20-30 minutes. But if you're using a stargazing app to help you navigate the night skies, that's not really an option. The good news is that, between individual stargazing apps and your phone's own built-in features, you can minimize the impact of your smartphone's screen light. How to block white light in stargazing apps SkyView and several other stargazing apps let you apply a red filter. (Image credit: Skyview) Many of the best stargazing apps will let you enable a red light filter or similar, though this option may not always be present in the free version. Here's how to do that in three of our favorite stargazing apps: SkyView : Tap the screen, tap the horizontal lines, tap on Settings, then Display, then Night Mode and Red. Star Walk 2 : Tap the horizontal lines, tap on Settings, then tap the button next to Night Mode. Sky Tonight: Tap the horizontal lines, tap on Settings, then Tools, then Night Mode. All these modes will minimize the amount of white light coming from the app. However, be aware that this is only within the app. Once you go back to your phone's main menu, it will be at full color. With the red screen naturally looking darker, you may have turned up the brightness on your phone, so making the switch away from the app will be quite the shock. If you want to dim your whole phone or put it into red light mode, here's how to do that on Android or iPhone . How to block white light on Android phones Many Android phones, including recent Pixel and Samsung models, include the equivalent of a red filter. (Image credit: Samsung) On Android, there are several ways to minimize the impact of bright light, depending on the model and make of phone you have. One near-universal option is to dim your smartphone. Swipe down the notification panel from the top of the screen and you'll see a brightness slider. Slide this to the left to dim your phone. We'd also recommend disabling adaptive brightness in the Display section of your phone's settings. You may also have an Extra Dim option in the Accessibility menu — just don't dim the screen to the point of not being able to see it at all! Some Android phones, such as recent Samsung and Google Pixel models, also offer a Red Filter. On some, you'll find this in Accessibility, then Vision Enhancements, then Color Filter. You can then choose the color you want and also tweak the opacity. All the above options will let you continue to use your smartphone for stargazing, while minimizing its negative impact on your night vision. How to block white light on Apple iPhones Apple's iPhones also offer an option to minimize the effect of white light. (Image credit: Apple) As with Android phones, iPhones have a built-in option to dim the screen brightness. In this case, you swipe down from the top of the screen and look for the vertical brightness slider, represented by a sun icon. Reduce the slider as much as you're comfortable with, dimming the screen while still keeping it visible. Beyond that, recent iPhones also offer the ability to apply a color filter, again via their Accessibility options. Here's how to do that. First, tap on the Settings icon, then pick Accessibility. Select Display & Text Size and go to Color Filters. Tap the Color Filter button. Then, pick Color Tint and move the Hue and Intensity sliders all the way to the right. We've got you covered with reviews and rankings of the best telescopes , binoculars , star projectors , cameras , drones , Lego , streaming and more.

item.title: We Explored Uganda With ADCCE 2026, From Lake Victoria to Murchison Falls | See Photos
item.description: One minute, you’re dressed up for a beautiful dinner overlooking Lake Victoria. A few days later, you’re on a safari, watching wildlife in its natural habitat, cruising along the River Nile and getting an up-close view of one of Uganda’s most famous waterfalls. That’s how our trip to Uganda went, and we have so much to tell you. We travelled to Uganda, popularly known as the Pearl of Africa, for the inaugural Africa Destination Celebrations Conference & Expo (ADCCE) 2026, held from 12 to 13 October at the Speke Resort Munyonyo Convention Centre in Kampala, with familiarisation trips following the conference. The theme, Africa Unveils Events in the Wild, was an invitation to explore Africa’s potential as a destination for weddings, celebrations, luxury travel and unforgettable experiences. And after spending five days between Kampala and Murchison Falls National Park, we got to experience some of that potential ourselves. Our BellaNaija crew consisted of Oluwadunsin Sanya , our Head of Editorial and Innovation, who also serves on ADCCE’s Board of Directors; Dorcas Anya , our Senior HR and Operations Associate; and me, Funmilola Sanya , Senior Content Associate. First Stop: Lake Victoria, New Connections and a Dinner to Remember Our ADCCE experience began right at the airport, where the team welcomed us warmly to Uganda. It was a lovely introduction to the trip, and we were ready to see what the days ahead had in store. We settled into Speke Resort Munyonyo, the conference venue, where event planners, wedding professionals, hospitality experts, tourism operators and creatives from different parts of Africa and beyond had gathered to connect and share ideas. Day one was all about business-to-business meetings, meeting industry professionals and exploring what the exhibitors had to offer. It was a great opportunity to make new connections and discover more about the possibilities for destination celebrations across Africa. Then came lunch at Sunset Restaurant, overlooking Lake Victoria. I had a whole tilapia fish with sides, while some of my fellow delegates opted for chicken. With delicious food and that beautiful lake view, lunch was certainly a lovely way to spend the afternoon. Later that evening, we gathered for the Sound of Africa Dinner. Dressed in smart-casual white, delegates had another opportunity to mingle, enjoy the music and dance. You know we weren’t going to travel all the way to Uganda and spend every evening sitting quietly. Between the conversations, music and laughter, it was a lovely start to our ADCCE adventure. item.content:encoded: One minute, you’re dressed up for a beautiful dinner overlooking Lake Victoria. A few days later, you’re on a safari, watching wildlife in its natural habitat, cruising along the River Nile and getting an up-close view of one of Uganda’s most famous waterfalls. We travelled to Uganda, popularly known as the Pearl of Africa, for the inaugural Africa Destination Celebrations Conference & Expo (ADCCE) 2026, held from 12 to 13 October at the Speke Resort Munyonyo Convention Centre in Kampala, with familiarisation trips following the conference. The theme, Africa Unveils Events in the Wild, was an invitation to explore Africa’s potential as a destination for weddings, celebrations, luxury travel and unforgettable experiences. And after spending five days between Kampala and Murchison Falls National Park, we got to experience some of that potential ourselves. Our BellaNaija crew consisted of Oluwadunsin Sanya , our Head of Editorial and Innovation, who also serves on ADCCE’s Board of Directors; Dorcas Anya , our Senior HR and Operations Associate; and me, Funmilola Sanya , Senior Content Associate. First Stop: Lake Victoria, New Connections and a Dinner to Remember Our ADCCE experience began right at the airport, where the team welcomed us warmly to Uganda. It was a lovely introduction to the trip, and we were ready to see what the days ahead had in store. We settled into Speke Resort Munyonyo, the conference venue, where event planners, wedding professionals, hospitality experts, tourism operators and creatives from different parts of Africa and beyond had gathered to connect and share ideas. Day one was all about business-to-business meetings, meeting industry professionals and exploring what the exhibitors had to offer. It was a great opportunity to make new connections and discover more about the possibilities for destination celebrations across Africa. Then came lunch at Sunset Restaurant, overlooking Lake Victoria. I had a whole tilapia fish with sides, while some of my fellow delegates opted for chicken. With delicious food and that beautiful lake view, lunch was certainly a lovely way to spend the afternoon. Later that evening, we gathered for the Sound of Africa Dinner. Dressed in smart-casual white, delegates had another opportunity to mingle, enjoy the music and dance. You know we weren’t going to travel all the way to Uganda and spend every evening sitting quietly. Between the conversations, music and laughter, it was a lovely start to our ADCCE adventure. Day Two: Big Conversations About Africa’s Celebration Industry The second day brought us back to the conference venue for conversations about positioning Africa as a global destination for celebrations. ADCCE founder Jackline Nanteza shared how attending a similar event had inspired her to believe that African event planners could one day come together to showcase the continent to the world. The first panel explored selling Destination Africa to the global market and the challenges of attracting international events. Oruonye Kingsley Chimezie championed Africa as a destination for celebrations, while Farah Lodhi reminded attendees, “What I believe is that in events, nothing is impossible as long as you don’t give up.” Rahul Soman highlighted how photography and social media can bring Africa’s destinations closer to couples worldwide, while Carol Matibiri reflected on the influence of international destination marketing. The second panel, “Uganda’s Event-Ready Hospitality Ecosystem,” moderated by Kemi Omeke , brought together representatives from NIRA, Uganda Tourism Board, Entikko Safari Lodge and UACII, alongside Frank Murangwa and Amos Wekesa , to discuss the partnerships needed to support events in Uganda. By evening, it was time for the black-tie VIP Networking Dinner, rounding off the conference with more opportunities to connect before our adventure continued into the wild. Next Stop: Murchison Falls National Park After the conference, we joined the familiarisation trip to Murchison Falls National Park. Getting there meant a long road trip from Kampala, filled with conversations, music courtesy of our DJ, Dorcas, laughter and Uganda’s changing scenery. We stayed at Entikko Safari Lodge, a beautiful retreat surrounded by nature. The food was another highlight, with so much to eat between our outings. Then came the safari the next morning. We spotted lions, giraffes, elephants, buffaloes and antelopes roaming the park. On our boat ride along the River Nile, we saw hippos and crocodiles in the water, offering us an even closer look at Uganda’s wildlife. Of course, we also visited Murchison Falls, often described as the world’s most powerful waterfall. Here, the River Nile squeezes through a gorge roughly seven metres wide before plunging about 43 metres. Seeing the rushing water and hearing its thunderous sound in person was an unforgettable experience. Between the wildlife, the breathtaking scenery and the delicious meals at Entikko, our Uganda adventure gave us plenty of memories to take home. One of my favourite parts of this trip was getting to experience Uganda with Oluwadunsin and Dorcas. Of course, we travelled for work, and ADCCE gave us the opportunity to meet professionals, learn about the destination celebrations industry and discover what different African businesses are creating. But there was also room to have fun together. We danced, laughed, explored new places, enjoyed the scenery and shared experiences that we’ll probably still be talking about long after returning home. And that’s one thing I appreciated about the structure of ADCCE 2026. The conference introduced us to the possibilities within Africa’s celebration and hospitality industries, while the familiarisation trip allowed us to see a destination beyond its meeting rooms and event venues. Uganda showed us its lakeside hospitality, its natural landscapes, its wildlife and some of the experiences that could make it an exciting choice for travellers and event organisers looking for something different. Until Next Time, Uganda! ADCCE 2026 brought together professionals with a shared interest in how Africa can welcome the world for celebrations, weddings, conferences and travel experiences. From the business conversations at Speke Resort Munyonyo to the adventures at Murchison Falls, the five-day experience gave us a lot to think about and even more to remember. We arrived in Uganda for a conference and left with new connections, fresh ideas, plenty of photographs and some wonderful travel memories. And if there’s one thing this trip has done, it’s given us even more reasons to explore Africa.
